16:I[12454,["/paper-daily-site/_next/static/chunks/08cykig6vtx_p.js","/paper-daily-site/_next/static/chunks/07qi2okp-.yp9.js","/paper-daily-site/_next/static/chunks/0frujd.eyhz4o.js","/paper-daily-site/_next/static/chunks/0n4z.7yu76je-.js","/paper-daily-site/_next/static/chunks/0otjhi71vbmnx.js","/paper-daily-site/_next/static/chunks/0j1uy9t~zxcf0.js","/paper-daily-site/_next/static/chunks/1304s0wcp2kce.js"],"WeeklyView"]
17:T4ff,The analysis uses the online-to-nonconvex conversion framework. The optimizer’s update rule is treated as an online learner, and the learner’s regret is converted into a Goldstein-style stationarity guarantee for nonsmooth nonconvex objectives. For a momentum matrix M = U Sigma V^T, the ideal Muon direction is the polar factor U V^T, which preserves singular subspaces and maps all positive singular values to one. This hard singular-value map is discontinuous. Finite Newton–Schulz replaces it with a polynomial map obtained by q iterations of an odd matrix polynomial, implemented with matrix multiplications rather than an SVD. The paper shows that this finite-depth map is the gradient of a smoothed spectral potential evaluated at the momentum matrix. This turns Muon into a gradient-based prediction algorithm. The discounted regret decomposes into a penalty term and a stability term. The penalty decreases as the smoothed potential approaches the nuclear norm; the stability term is controlled by the Lipschitz constant of the finite Newton–Schulz map. Choosing q = O(log(1/epsilon)) balances these terms. The key conceptual move is to use the finite-depth deviation from the exact polar factor as smoothing, rather than treating it only as approximation error.18:T467,The baseline objective interpolates standard next-token cross-entropy with a KL term between temperature-scaled teacher and student next-token distributions. The paper studies both forward KL and reverse KL, varying teacher size and the interpolation coefficient. The central analysis uses teacher predictive entropy as a diagnostic. Low-entropy teacher predictions tend to appear on procedural or highly constrained tokens, where the teacher distribution is sharp and informative. High-entropy predictions are common on unstructured web text and factual continuations with many plausible next tokens. In high-entropy regions, KD reduces the relative force of the one-hot ground-truth token compared with NTP, so it can slow the learning of facts that the student has not yet acquired. Switch Distillation follows directly from this analysis: use KD on low-entropy tokens and fall back to NTP on high-entropy tokens. The routing signal comes from the same teacher logits already needed for KD, so the method adds little overhead and differs from global fixes such as tuning alpha, changing KL direction, or scaling the teacher.19:T466,The controlled experiments use the OLMo-2 ecosystem, with 1B students and larger 7B/13B teachers, including instruction-tuned teachers. In pre-training, forward-KL distillation improves reasoning and factual recall over vanilla NTP. In mid-training, increasing distillation strength generally improves reasoning but hurts factual recall relative to NTP. This pattern is robust across teacher sizes, KL directions, and interpolation coefficients; no conventional KD objective Pareto-dominates NTP in mid-training. The entropy analysis supports the mechanism: teacher entropy varies strongly by data type, lower entropy correlates with higher-quality supervision, and the facts not yet learned at the start of mid-training tend to receive weaker teacher supervision. Switch Distillation improves the tradeoff. With an OLMo-2 7B Instruct teacher, it raises average reasoning by 71% and knowledge/commonsense by 19% over NTP, while reducing factual recall by only about 1 percentage point. After post-training, the gains persist: reasoning remains 32% higher, knowledge tasks improve by 20%, and the factual recall gap disappears.1a:T448,The core metric is Token Economy Score, TES(Mr, Mb, T) = [Acc(Mr,T) - Acc(Mb,T)] / [GenTok(Mr,T) / GenTok(Mb,T)]. Mr is the reasoning-enabled model, Mb is the non-reasoning baseline, and GenTok is reasoning tokens plus final answer tokens. Input tokens are deliberately excluded because they are mostly determined by the benchmark prompt and evaluation harness rather than by the model’s reasoning behavior. TES is therefore a marginal metric, unlike absolute accuracy-per-token metrics such as Per-Token Intelligence. TES greater than 1 means the accuracy gain in percentage points exceeds the generated-token multiplier; values between 0 and 1 indicate positive but weak marginal efficiency; values at or below 0 indicate that reasoning is wasteful or damaging. The paper also defines deployment-facing quantities, including Reasoning Cost Share and Deployment Cost Multiplier, to connect token behavior with cloud and on-premises cost profiles. A key caveat is explicit: TES is a practical convention, not a universal utility function, and should be read with baseline and absolute accuracy.1b:T867,The setup is simple and clean. Given a pretrained model of size N and a total annotation budget B, an allocation ratio r sends rB examples to SFT and (1-r)B to RL. Performance is written as P(N, r, B; tau). A standard formulation would optimize r* = argmax_r P, but the paper argues that this is the wrong target because post-training curves are often flat near the top. A tiny gain in measured score may not justify a full retraining run, and the exact argmax can be unstable under noise. The paper therefore defines the epsilon-near-optimal region: the set of ratios whose performance is at least (1-epsilon) times the best observed performance.

This shift enables three analyses. First, region characterization: the authors sweep allocation ratios across tasks, model families, and RL methods, then measure how wide the near-optimal region is under tolerances such as 2% to 10%. Second, scale transfer: instead of asking whether the exact optimum ratio matches across scales, they ask whether the near-optimal region found on a small proxy model covers high-performing ratios on a larger model. This is a much more stable transfer criterion. Third, asymmetric annotation cost: the default setup measures budget in number of labeled examples, but the paper extends the framework to cases where SFT and RL labels have different unit costs. Under that view, the effective optimum shifts, and the acceptable region can widen further when SFT data is relatively more expensive.

Relative to prior work, the novelty is in the problem formulation and the transfer criterion. Earlier work mostly reported broad trends, such as SFT being more important in low-data regimes and preference optimization becoming more useful at larger scales, but did not provide a principled near-optimal allocation framework or establish transfer from small to large models. Work on data mixture optimization and scaling-law extrapolation usually focuses on single-stage training, especially pretraining mixtures, not sequential SFT-then-RL coupling. The paper’s contribution is to turn a brittle tuning problem into a region-finding problem with practical transfer value.1c:T6f4,The most important empirical findings are structural rather than benchmark-centric. First, the performance-versus-allocation curve typically has a broad plateau near its maximum. Even with small tolerances, such as a few percent from peak performance, the near-optimal region is already wide. Second, this region generally widens with model scale. Larger models are therefore more forgiving to imperfect SFT/RL splits. Third, transfer works better at the region level than at the exact-optimum level: a near-optimal region identified on a small proxy model tends to reliably contain high-performing allocations for a larger target model, even when the exact best ratio shifts. Fourth, the pattern is observed across tasks, model families, and both off-policy and on-policy RL settings, which argues against the effect being tied to one specific algorithm.

The paper also includes a useful cost sanity check. Using measured runtimes and L40S cloud pricing, per-example training compute cost is reported to range from about 2e-5 USD for the cheapest 1B SFT setting to about 3e-4 USD for 8B DPO. Compared with human annotation costs around 0.5 to 1.0 USD per example, compute is lower by roughly three to five orders of magnitude. Even compared with cheap synthetic annotation around 1e-3 USD per example, compute is still usually below annotation. This supports the paper’s decision to treat annotation as the dominant first-order budget axis.

The paper is less about headline absolute scores and more about curve geometry, region width, and transfer coverage. When reading the experiments, the key is not the single best number but how flat the top is, how the width changes with scale, and how much overlap exists between proxy-model and target-model high-performance regions.1d:T563,Start with the introduction and preliminaries. The central conceptual move is the replacement of exact optimality with near-optimality. If that framing makes sense, the rest of the paper becomes straightforward. Then focus on the sections that define and analyze the near-optimal region. The most informative figures are the allocation-performance curves, the region-width comparisons across scales, and the small-to-large transfer plots. In those figures, do not over-focus on the exact argmax. Look at plateau width and overlap.

The most useful sections to read carefully are the ones corresponding to region analysis, scale transfer, and asymmetric annotation cost. Those sections answer three practical questions: why a region is a better target than a point, why small proxy experiments can replace large-scale search, and how the framework changes when SFT and RL labels have different prices. It is also worth checking how tolerance is defined, how noisy training outcomes are handled, and what criterion is used to claim reliable transfer. The paper’s main value lies in recipe design logic, not in a new optimizer or RL objective. Anyone working on large-scale training pipelines can reuse the same lens for other multi-stage allocation problems, including continual pretraining versus SFT, SFT versus preference data, or allocation across multiple RL signal sources.1e:T4e7,The method, VIG-Sampler, is built on two empirical observations. First, candidate tokens that place stronger attention on image tokens tend to be both better grounded in the visual input and more useful for predicting the remaining masked tokens. Based on this, the sampler uses token-level image attention as the ordering score, prioritizing visually informative tokens over high-confidence but semantically weak ones. Second, when multiple tokens are decoded in parallel, their individual information gains do not add up cleanly because some of them are redundant. The paper argues that this redundancy is reflected in similar token-to-image attention distributions. VIG-Sampler therefore adds a similarity-based penalty during subset selection: if a candidate attends to the image in a way that is too similar to already selected tokens, its priority is reduced. This gives a simple two-part design: image-attention-based ranking for grounding, plus attention-similarity penalty for complementary information. Compared with certainty-based samplers, it avoids locking in punctuation, copulas, or other frequent low-content tokens too early. Compared with text-only info-gain samplers, it explicitly injects visual evidence into the decoding trajectory.1f:Ta22,方法核心是“自参考的局部分支探索 + signed distillation”。在某个 on-policy 时间步 t_j，模型先按当前 ODE 预测得到一个确定性的下一状态；然后从同一个父状态出发，额外分出 K 个带噪声的 SDE 候选分支。每个分支只在当前步做随机探索，之后再用确定性 ODE 一路 rollout 到干净图像。这样做的目的很明确：把当前局部方向的好坏，转化为最终图像奖励的差异。

为了把终局奖励变成局部监督，作者同时从同一父状态做一条 deterministic ODE rollout 作为 baseline。每个分支最终得到的 reward 与 baseline reward 做比较，形成 normalized branch advantage。这样 advantage 不是绝对分数，而是“从当前状态出发，这个局部扰动比默认走法更好还是更差”。这一步很关键，因为它把不同 prompt、不同 reward 量纲、不同时间步上的分数差异压成了可比较的局部相对信号。

训练目标不是只拉近最好分支，而是 all-branch pull-push distillation。高 advantage 分支把当前 velocity field 拉向更优局部方向；低 advantage 分支则把模型从差方向上推开。相比只学 best-of-K，这种 signed objective 利用了更多探索样本，样本效率更高，也更像一个局部排序学习问题。但 signed update 容易不稳，尤其是“推开差分支”可能与“靠近好分支”方向冲突。为此作者加了 direction-aware attenuation：如果某个 repulsive update 会明显抵消 best branch 的主方向，就衰减其权重，避免训练在局部几何上自相矛盾。

另一个技术点是 SDE-variance normalization。因为不同时间步、不同噪声强度下，SDE 分支的位移尺度不同，若直接回归分支目标，loss 尺度会失衡。作者用 SDE 方差做归一化，使每步监督更接近统一量纲，并给出与 reward-tilted KL 最小化相关的解释：模型在每个局部状态附近，把概率质量往高奖励分支倾斜。

多目标部分也值得注意。已有一些 OPD 方法会为不同目标训练不同 teacher，再在 field level 做路由或融合。Self-OPD 不这么做。它先把多个 reward 归一化后在 scalar reward 层融合，只用融合后的分数对局部分支排序；真正回归的对象仍然是某条具体分支对应的 velocity target，而不是多个 teacher field 的线性组合。这样避免了不同目标梯度直接打架，也更符合“同一张图同时满足多个约束”的目标，而不是不同 teacher 各自擅长不同样本。20:T953,The method is built around self-referenced local branching plus signed distillation. At an on-policy step t_j, the current model first predicts the deterministic next state along the ODE trajectory. From the same parent state, it then spawns K stochastic SDE branches. Each branch explores only locally at the current step, after which it is rolled out deterministically to a clean image. The purpose is to evaluate whether a local directional perturbation leads to a better final sample.

A deterministic ODE rollout from the same parent state serves as a self-reference baseline. Final rewards from the K branches are compared against this baseline reward to produce normalized branch advantages. This is important because the signal becomes relative and local: not whether a sample is globally good, but whether a local move from the current state is better or worse than the default trajectory.

Training uses an all-branch pull-push distillation objective. Positive-advantage branches pull the velocity field toward better local directions, while negative-advantage branches push it away from poor ones. Compared with only regressing toward the best branch, this uses more of the sampled neighborhood and turns local exploration into a richer ranking signal. The downside is potential instability: repulsive updates can conflict with attractive ones. To address that, the paper introduces direction-aware attenuation, which downweights repulsion when it would substantially cancel the direction of the best branch.

Another key component is SDE-variance normalization. Since branch displacement scales vary across timesteps and noise levels, direct regression would produce poorly calibrated losses. Normalizing by SDE variance makes the per-step target more comparable across the trajectory and is connected in the paper to a reward-tilted KL view: locally shifting probability mass toward higher-reward branches.

For multi-objective alignment, Self-OPD avoids field-level fusion of multiple teachers. Instead, it normalizes and combines scalar rewards first, uses the composite reward only to rank branches, and still regresses toward a concrete trajectory-derived velocity target. This is cleaner for black-box rewards and better aligned with the actual goal: one image satisfying multiple constraints simultaneously, rather than separate experts excelling on different samples.21:T55d,The experimental story, based on the provided full-text sections, is centered on single-reward and mixed-reward alignment, with comparisons against two families of baselines: direct RL methods and teacher-based OPD methods. The paper reports that Self-OPD outperforms both, with the advantage being especially visible in mixed-reward settings where one model is expected to satisfy text rendering, compositional correctness, and aesthetics at the same time.

The most informative comparisons are likely the following: (1) single-reward versus mixed-reward performance, to test whether the method really resolves objective conflict; (2) training stability against teacher-free RL, to validate the dense-supervision claim; (3) performance against teacher-based OPD, to test whether removing the teacher sacrifices or improves alignment quality; and (4) ablations on branch count K, pull-only versus pull-push, direction-aware attenuation, and reward fusion strategy.

The excerpt does not include the full result tables, model sizes, compute budget, or exact benchmark numbers, so it would be unsafe to invent precise gains. The numbers worth checking in the full paper are the reward improvements over RL baselines, whether all component rewards improve simultaneously under mixed objectives, and whether removing push or attenuation causes clear degradation or instability.22:T44c,GRAS combines two changes. First, it improves the guided proposal. Prior GILC-style methods correct clean-token logits with a straight-through reward gradient, but the gradient is often estimated from a single noisy sample. For differentiable rewards, GRAS uses a Gumbel-Rao / Rao-Blackwellized reveal estimator to analytically average part of the reveal randomness and reduce variance. For non-differentiable rewards, it uses a leave-one-out baseline to reduce particle-level reward noise. These proposal changes add no denoiser calls. Second, it changes the search stage. Standard SMC/TDS-like resampling often uses a fixed temperature, although the spread of values differs across denoising steps. GRAS introduces AMC, an adaptive-temperature resampling rule that standardizes per-step values into group-relative advantages and lets a single scale parameter control selection pressure. Compared with simply stacking gradient guidance and search, the useful contribution is the accounting framework: variance reduction, adaptive selection, diversity cost, and denoiser budget are analyzed together.23:T7e8,The proposed solution is RecursiveGPT, built around two ideas. The first is factorized embeddings, which reduce the share of parameters spent on the input and output vocabulary maps. This matters because when hidden size is reduced, Transformer block parameters shrink roughly quadratically, while embedding-related parameters shrink much more slowly. As a result, small standard LMs can spend a disproportionate fraction of capacity on token lookup rather than sequence computation.

The second idea is recursive weight sharing across depth. Instead of stacking many independently parameterized Transformer blocks, the model repeatedly applies a shared block for multiple recurrent steps. This increases the amount of computation performed on each token without a proportional increase in parameter count. The paper is explicit that this is not mainly a compute-efficiency argument in the serving sense; it is a way to scale computation under fixed data while keeping model size under control.

Architecturally, this is closer to ALBERT-style cross-layer sharing plus recurrent refinement than to a new sequence model family. The interesting questions are therefore in the implementation details: how many recursive steps to use, how to stabilize training with shared blocks and residual connections, whether step information is encoded explicitly, and how to choose the factorization dimension for embeddings. The paper studies these choices systematically in a BabyLM-like setup rather than presenting a single tuned model.

A notable aspect of the work is what it does not rely on. It does not primarily solve overfitting through aggressive recipe engineering such as unusually large weight decay, elaborate stopping heuristics, or late ensembling. Nor does it switch to a different objective such as masked LM or diffusion-style masked modeling. The claim is narrower and cleaner: even with a conventional causal LM objective, architecture alone can improve the compute–parameter trade-off in the limited-data regime.24:T863,The experiments span roughly 10M to 100M words, model sizes from about 13M to 1.2B parameters, two corpora, and several evaluations including BabyLM-relevant benchmarks such as BLiMP and COMPS, with supplementary reporting on BLiMP Supplement, EWoK, and Entity Tracking. The most important result is not a single score but the shape of the scaling behavior.

First, there is a clear optimal model size, and that optimum depends strongly on both the data budget and the evaluation target. The best size at 10M words is not the same as at 100M words, and different downstream or linguistic evaluations prefer different scales. That is a strong empirical reminder that “bigger is better” does not transfer cleanly into the low-data regime.

Second, the paper shows that standard Transformers use parameters inefficiently when scaled down. As models get smaller, the fraction of parameters tied up in embeddings and the LM head rises sharply, while performance does not improve monotonically with total parameter count. Past a certain point, training loss may continue to decrease while validation and downstream metrics deteriorate. RecursiveGPT improves on matched standard Transformer baselines by allocating more of the budget to token transformation rather than to independent parameters.

Third, RecursiveGPT outperforms standard Transformer baselines at both 10M and 100M word budgets and remains competitive with strong BabyLM 2025 systems. The abstract does not list all numbers, but the body emphasizes consistent gains across the main evaluations. The ablations are important: both factorized embeddings and recursive depth help, but the larger benefit comes from adding computation through shared-depth recurrence rather than merely shrinking vocabulary maps.

Fourth, the training-dynamics analysis is useful. The paper documents the overfitting pattern directly: larger models fit the training corpus better but generalize worse, while recursive models make better use of extra compute under the same data budget. For researchers interested in limited-data scaling, these curves are more informative than the leaderboard comparisons.25:Tac2,LoGo 的核心设计是每层同时有 local 和 global 两个分支，但两者不是两套完全独立的大模块。所有 token 都先走 local attention，只看一个受限窗口；global 分支只对被选中的 query 激活，被选中的 token 再把 local/global 输出做融合，未选中的 token 直接绕过 global 分支。这样做的关键点有四个。

第一，动态分配单位是 token，而不是层或头。论文把 attention span 当作 attention budget 的代理变量：一个 token 是否需要全局上下文，可以由当前隐藏状态预测。具体做法是用一个轻量 gate 为每个 token 产生标量偏好分数，表示它对 global span 的需求。

第二，路由不是固定阈值，而是自适应阈值控制全局激活比例。作者设定 target global ratio，在每个 batch 或序列内根据 gate 分数确定阈值，把 top-ratio 的 token 送入 global 分支。这样可以把计算预算直接绑定到“有多少 token 走全局”，而不是让 gate 自由漂移导致预算失控。相比用连续权重软混合，这种二值路由更容易把理论 FLOPs 节省转成真实 kernel 加速。

第三，训练时用了 progressive mask，也就是文中说的 P-mask。问题在于如果一开始就做硬路由，gate 还没学到有意义的偏好，容易让训练不稳定，或者过早把重要 token 切掉。LoGo 在训练早期延迟引入稀疏路由，先让 local/global 结构和 gate 有一个较平滑的学习阶段，再逐步过渡到目标稀疏度。这一点很像 conditional computation 里常见的 warmup/annealing 思路，但这里作用在 attention routing 上。

第四，只稀疏 global queries，不稀疏 KV。也就是说，所有 token 的 key/value 仍然保留在全局可见集合里，只是并非每个 query 都去访问它们。这样被选中的 token 仍然拥有精确的 full-context attention，而不是近似检索或压缩记忆；代价则主要按被选中 query 数量下降。这个设计比同时稀疏 query 和 KV 更稳，因为不会破坏信息可达性，也避免了额外的 memory selection 误差。

从与现有方法的区别看，静态 inter-layer hybrid 是某些层全局、某些层局部；intra-layer hybrid 是某些头全局、某些头局部；它们都把预算结构写死了。LoGo 则让同一层内不同 token 走不同 span。与 CoLT5、SMA 这类动态模块激活方法相比，LoGo 直接把“是否需要长程上下文”作为路由目标，而不是切换不同 attention 模块或受限 span 模块。工程上，作者还实现了 query-sparse Triton kernel，把只对部分 query 做 global attention 的结构真正映射到运行时加速，而不是停留在 FLOPs 账面节省。26:Ta3b,LoGo builds each attention layer from coupled local and global branches. Every token always receives local attention over a restricted window. A lightweight gate predicts, for each token, whether global span is worth paying for. Selected tokens additionally go through the global branch and fuse local/global outputs; unselected tokens bypass the global branch entirely.

There are four important design choices.

First, the routing unit is the token. The paper explicitly uses attention span as a proxy for attention budget: if a token likely depends on long-range retrieval, it should be allowed to access the full sequence; if it is locally predictable, local context is enough. This differs from static layer-wise or head-wise span assignment.

Second, routing is controlled by an adaptive threshold tied to a target global ratio. Instead of using a fixed threshold or unconstrained soft gating, LoGo selects roughly the top fraction of tokens for global attention. This keeps compute predictable and directly links routing decisions to budget. It also makes it easier to convert FLOP savings into real speedups, because the global branch becomes query-sparse in a hard, structured way.

Third, training uses progressive masking (P-mask). Hard sparse routing from the start would make optimization brittle because the gate is initially untrained and may suppress important tokens too early. LoGo therefore delays the full sparse regime and gradually introduces routing sparsity after the gate has learned more meaningful preferences. This is a training-stability device, and it is one of the more important parts of the method.

Fourth, LoGo sparsifies only global queries, not keys or values. All KV states remain globally available, so any selected token still performs exact full-context attention rather than an approximation over compressed memory. This is a conservative but sensible design: it reduces compute without damaging information accessibility.

Relative to prior work, static inter-layer hybrids assign some layers to global attention and others to local attention; intra-layer hybrids assign some heads to global and others to local. Both impose a fixed per-token budget. LoGo instead lets different tokens in the same layer take different span routes. Compared with dynamic module activation methods such as CoLT5 or SMA, LoGo directly routes based on span demand rather than swapping among attention modules with the same restricted context. On the systems side, the paper also implements query-sparse Triton kernels so the reduced global-attention workload translates into actual runtime gains.27:T695,The experiments are organized around three claims.

First, scaling behavior. The authors train models from 200M up to 3.3B parameters and report that LoGo consistently matches or slightly improves over a standard Transformer on language modeling. This matters because many dynamic-routing ideas look promising only at small scale; once moved into real pretraining regimes, instability or routing overhead often erases the benefit. Here the evidence suggests token-level span allocation does not break backbone scalability.

Second, matched-budget comparisons at around 1.5B scale. Under matched parameter count and attention FLOPs, LoGo is compared against a standard Transformer and static inter-layer and intra-layer local-global hybrids. The main result is a better performance-compute trade-off: strongest language-modeling results among the compared variants, competitive short-context recall, and clearer gains on long-range retrieval after context extension. The emphasis is not just raw quality, but quality at the same budget.

Third, implementation and ablations. Kernel benchmarks show that the query-sparse Triton implementation delivers practical speedups that are close to the theoretical FLOP reduction at long sequence lengths. Ablations cover progressive masking, adaptive thresholding, the target global ratio, and compatibility with static hybrids. Two takeaways stand out: performance is reasonably robust across global ratios, and LoGo can be combined with static hybrids to reduce both memory and compute. The analysis section also reports interpretable routing patterns, with tokens that require long-range access being selected more often for the global branch.28:T45a,For a skim-level read, start with the introduction and Figure 1. The key idea is not generic sparse attention, but token-level span allocation with span treated as the budget proxy.

Then read the method sections on the gate, adaptive threshold, and progressive masking. The most useful questions are why the model needs a target global ratio, and why hard routing cannot be turned on from the beginning. Those choices explain most of the training and systems behavior.

In the experiments, prioritize three items: the scaling plots, the matched-budget 1.5B comparison table, and the kernel benchmark. Together they answer whether the method preserves Transformer-like scaling, whether it beats static hybrids under fair budgets, and whether the FLOP savings become real speedups. If time is limited, the most informative ablations are the ones on P-mask, global ratio, and the combination with static hybrids.

A solid skim should take about 25 to 35 minutes. If your work touches long-context backbones or conditional computation, the appendix is worth checking for implementation details and routing statistics.29:T778,The paper has two technical components: a measurement framework and a decoding intervention.

For measurement, the authors build a step-wise and position-wise analysis framework for masked diffusion language models. At each denoising step, the model predicts clean-token distributions for all positions, but only a subset of still-masked positions is committed. Using this structure, the paper tracks refusal-related token mass across denoising steps and response positions under harmful prompts. It distinguishes several events: whether refusal evidence appears at all, whether refusal tokens are committed, whether that commitment persists or gets overwritten, and how early commitments affect the final safety outcome.

This leads to the paper’s main conceptual finding: shallow-step alignment. The claim is that early denoising steps themselves form a safety-sensitive axis in dLLMs. Tokens committed early can strongly influence the final safety outcome even when they are not all at the leading response positions. Compared with shallow alignment in autoregressive models, diffusion models introduce an additional temporal dimension tied to denoising rather than surface order.

Based on that analysis, the paper proposes Refusal-Aware Early Commitment (RAEC), a training-free decoding method. RAEC changes only the commitment decision during decoding. If a refusal signal appears early and remains sufficiently strong and persistent, the decoder commits it early before later denoising dynamics can wash it out. Importantly, RAEC does not inject an external refusal template; it acts on refusal probability mass already produced by the model. This design is well matched to the diagnosed failure mode. If unsafe trajectories often contain weak or transient refusal evidence, then intervening at commitment time is a more targeted fix than retraining the model or attaching an external safety classifier.2a:T6fc,The evaluation uses harmful-instruction benchmarks including JailbreakBench and StrongREJECT, with Llama-Guard-3-8B as the safety judge and Attack Success Rate (ASR) as the main metric. The tested models include masked diffusion LMs such as LLaDA and Dream.

The empirical findings come in three layers. First, the measurement results show that refusal signals are concentrated in early denoising steps and leading response positions, but these are not the same thing. Early-step commitments have a strong effect on final safety, supporting the shallow-step alignment hypothesis. The paper also includes intervention-style analyses: forcing early refusal commitment makes an unaligned base dLLM safer, while forcing early compliance commitment can push an aligned model toward unsafe outputs. That suggests early commitment is not just correlated with safety; it is a causal control point.

Second, the paper analyzes unsafe trajectories and finds that many of them do contain refusal evidence. The issue is that the refusal mass is weak, transient, or overwritten before commitment. Safe trajectories, in contrast, show stronger and more persistent refusal mass and much higher refusal-commitment rates. This is an important mechanistic refinement: the failure is often not “no refusal capability,” but “refusal evidence does not survive to commitment.”

Third, RAEC reduces ASR on both LLaDA and Dream while largely preserving utility. The provided text does not include the full result tables, so it would be unsafe to quote exact deltas here. When reading the original paper, the key numbers to verify are the ASR reductions on each benchmark, the utility trade-off on benign prompts, and the sensitivity to the thresholds controlling early commitment and refusal persistence.2b:T57f,This is a good skim paper for readers interested in mechanism rather than only safety application. If reading more deeply, pair the intervention experiments with the ablations.2c:T445,The authors formulate variable-length generation in a padded sequence space with an absorbing empty token, so autoregressive decoding can be viewed as a time-dependent transport from the empty sequence to complete samples. They then define a family of target distributions derived from the base LLM, including powered distributions for sharpening, product distributions for combining constraints, and tilted distributions using additional potentials. Two sampling algorithms are proposed. The Sequential Monte Carlo variant maintains a population of particles along an annealing path and uses importance weights plus resampling to avoid the degeneracy of one-shot importance sampling. The Replica Exchange variant runs chains at different temperatures or sharpness levels and swaps states across replicas, allowing high-temperature chains to explore while low-temperature chains focus on high-probability regions. Compared with Best-of-N, these methods use intermediate distributions and adaptive weighting rather than drawing many independent base-model samples and filtering them afterwards.2d:T76c,The main idea is affix-oriented cache reuse. Instead of restricting reuse to shared prefixes, the paper generalizes it to any shared contiguous span, or affix, which may appear at the beginning, middle, or end of the context. This is a natural systems opportunity created by bidirectional attention: unlike AR models, DLLMs are not inherently prefix-centric.

The key challenge is deciding which affix-token KV states become meaningfully stale as the masked generation tokens evolve. ACache introduces Anchor Tokens for this purpose. It measures the cross-attention importance from masked generation tokens to affix tokens, identifies a small request-specific subset of influential affix tokens, and recomputes KV states only for those anchors. The remaining affix-token cache is reused. In effect, the method turns a coarse full-span refresh decision into a sparse token-level refresh decision.

Implementation-wise, ACache is built on top of Fast-dLLM. It replaces periodic full-cache recomputation with selective anchor-token recomputation, so it is an incremental but targeted improvement over existing approximate caching frameworks rather than a completely new inference stack. The authors also implement a shared-prefix prototype in Nano-vLLM to test whether the gains survive under a more realistic serving environment with paged memory management and continuous batching.

Relative to prior work, the distinction is clear. dLLM-Cache uses asymmetric prompt/response refresh and feature-similarity-based partial recomputation for response tokens. dKV-Cache focuses more on decoded-token reuse with delayed block recomputation. Fast-dLLM improves the overall inference framework but still relies on periodic refresh. ACache is novel in treating shared context itself as the optimization target and shrinking the recomputation unit from an entire shared span to a request-specific token subset.2e:T504,The main results operate at three levels. First, quality recovery: compared with direct affix-cache reuse, which causes noticeable degradation, ACache recovers most of the lost accuracy across multiple benchmarks while recomputing only around 20% of affix tokens. That number matters because it suggests the stale-cache problem is sparse enough to be exploitable. Second, system gains: in the Nano-vLLM shared-prefix prototype, ACache reduces recomputation latency by up to 55.7% and improves end-to-end throughput by up to 1.68x. This indicates that the benefit is not just a FLOP-level argument but can survive a realistic serving stack. Third, scope: the method applies to shared spans beyond prefixes, which is practically relevant because reusable text in production often appears as retrieved snippets, tool outputs, templates, or summarized dialogue history rather than only as a left prefix.

For a researcher, the most informative part is likely the ablation structure rather than any single headline number: how stable the anchor-selection rule is, how quality changes as the recomputation ratio varies, whether affix position matters, and how stale-cache error accumulates across denoising steps. If the paper includes those plots, they are the ones worth studying closely.2f:T598,TwinKV defines importance through pairwise redundancy in key space. For each token, it counts how many non-adjacent tokens have a key vector with cosine similarity above a fixed threshold. A high twin count means the token is redundant; a low count means it is likely unique and harder to recover if evicted. Two design choices matter. First, the method operates on keys rather than values or hidden states, because eviction affects what can later be retrieved through attention, and keys are the retrieval addresses. Second, it excludes adjacent tokens to avoid trivial local similarity from contiguous text.

The more interesting systems idea is to use TwinKV as a repair pass rather than a standalone eviction policy. Given any existing method’s retained and evicted sets under a fixed budget, TwinKV looks for two types of mismatch: an evicted token with no surviving near-duplicate, and a retained token whose information is already duplicated among retained tokens. It then swaps them while keeping the budget unchanged. This is a low-intrusion design: it does not need the wrapped method’s internal scores, only its final keep set. The paper also distinguishes this from anchor-based approaches that score keys by distance from a single global reference point. Those methods measure outlierness relative to a centroid; TwinKV measures substitutability through local pairwise relations. That is a different inductive bias.30:T623,The experiments answer two questions. First, does attention track causal utility? Using chunk-level leave-one-out on real long-context QA, the authors measure how much removing a chunk hurts the log-probability of the correct answer and compare that with the chunk’s attention mass in the original forward pass. The correlation is effectively zero, which directly weakens the premise behind attention-based eviction.

Second, does TwinKV improve existing policies as a post-hoc repair? On Qwen3-4B, the method is composed with four recent eviction baselines: StreamingLLM, PyramidKV, SnapKV, and ExpectedAttention. Evaluation covers LongBench, LooGLE, RULER, and a short-context MMLU-Pro control set, at compression ratios 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7. The gains are conditional rather than universal: TwinKV improves a majority of evaluated cells for StreamingLLM (up to 64% of cells) and PyramidKV (57%), is closer to neutral for SnapKV (41%), and helps only a minority for ExpectedAttention (16%). The paper argues that ExpectedAttention is already near ceiling on several settings, leaving more room for harmful perturbation than for correction. Another consistent pattern is that TwinKV helps more under tighter budgets; at the loosest compression ratio, average gains are smallest. That fits the paper’s causal story: when every retained slot matters, preserving unique information becomes more valuable.

The empirical emphasis is on breadth of positive configurations and compatibility with multiple baselines, not on a single large absolute score jump on one benchmark.31:T49a,Start with the introduction and Figure 1. The study covers two representative MLLMs: Wan2.2 for multimodal generation and Qwen3-VL for multimodal reasoning. It evaluates multiple low-precision formats, including MXFP8, MXFP4, and HiF4, across a wide set of components: vision encoders, text encoders, attention blocks, feed-forward layers, multimodal projection layers, and MoE modules. The analysis shows that FP8 is nearly lossless, while FP4 degradation is highly heterogeneous. In Wan2.2, the visual generation backbone is the main bottleneck and the UMT5 text encoder is relatively robust. In Qwen3-VL, the vision encoder is especially sensitive, though the language backbone also degrades under FP4. Crucially, ablations separating weight-only from activation quantization indicate that activation quantization is the dominant source of performance loss.

Based on this diagnosis, the paper proposes Residual Fallback Quantization (RFQ). Unlike threshold-based outlier fallback methods, which detect large values and route them through a higher-precision path, RFQ uses a fully low-bit and differentiable decomposition. It first quantizes the activation into a primary FP4 representation, then explicitly computes the quantization residual and sends that residual through a secondary low-bit quantization path for reconstruction. Conceptually, the approximation is q(x) + q_res(x - q(x)), rather than a hard split between normal values and outliers.

This design has several practical advantages. It is differentiable and suitable for end-to-end training. It avoids threshold tuning, which is difficult when outlier behavior varies by module and evolves during training. It does not require full-precision fallback, making it more compatible with true FP4 execution. And because it models the current quantization error directly, it is better aligned with dynamic training-time activation statistics than PTQ-style calibration methods.

Methodologically, RFQ sits between static PTQ smoothing and mixed-precision QAT fallback. It accepts that FP4 cannot faithfully represent the full activation range in many MLLM modules, and therefore models the error instead of forcing the original distribution through a single quantizer.33:T644,From the provided full text, several empirical conclusions are already clear.

1. Precision formats separate cleanly in quality: MXFP8 is close to lossless, while MXFP4 and HiF4 incur substantial degradation. This suggests that 8-bit training/deployment is already fairly mature for current MLLMs, whereas 4-bit remains the hard regime.
2. Activation quantization hurts much more than weight quantization. The paper runs extensive ablations to isolate their contributions, and the main takeaway is that compressing weights alone is often manageable, but pushing activations to FP4 causes the major collapse.
3. Sensitivity is strongly module-dependent. In Wan2.2, the WanDiT visual generation backbone is the main failure point, while the text encoder is relatively stable. In Qwen3-VL, the vision encoder is the most sensitive, though language modules are not immune. This argues against a single uniform quantization strategy across the whole MLLM stack.
4. RFQ recovers a meaningful portion of the FP4 loss without using high-precision fallback. The abstract excerpt does not provide exact numbers, but the framing makes clear that RFQ primarily addresses activation-outlier-induced instability rather than offering a small average gain everywhere.

If the full paper includes detailed tables, the most informative numbers to inspect are the relative gaps among FP8, FP4, and HiF4 on both generation and reasoning tasks, and the decomposition into weight-only, activation-only, and joint quantization. For pretraining researchers, those diagnostics are more useful than a single final benchmark score.34:T574,Read this paper with diagnosis first and method second. Rows of the output embedding matrix are treated as token vectors, and the final hidden state is used as the query. Instead of evaluating all logits, the system retrieves likely high-score tokens using an approximate nearest-neighbor index. The authors evaluate FAISS-backed options and choose HNSW because it offers the best latency–recall trade-off in this high-dimensional embedding space. The index is built post-training from the static output embeddings and can be distributed with the checkpoint. At inference time, the HNSW ef parameter controls the speed–accuracy trade-off. To reduce harmful misses, the implementation explicitly scores selected special tokens, common punctuation, and structural words. Retrieved logits can be scattered into a sparse full-vocabulary tensor, which keeps the method compatible with existing decoding pipelines. Unlike Adaptive Softmax-style designs, this does not require architectural changes during pretraining.36:T4bc,The method represents the CFG as a pushdown automaton. A PDA configuration consists of a finite control state and an unbounded stack. To handle tokenizer–grammar mismatch, the online state is extended to (q, gamma, rho), where rho stores the open prefix of a grammar terminal currently being matched. Offline, the method builds bounded stack summaries under a stack-height limit H and computes reachability-to-acceptance labels using Pre*-style saturation from pushdown-system analysis. It then turns the PDA into a weighted pushdown system. A terminal-consuming transition is assigned the minimum number of LLM tokens needed to generate that terminal; for regex terminals, the method first picks a shortest string in the regex language and computes its minimum tokenization length. Epsilon transitions have zero cost. These computations produce token-level upper-bound distances to acceptance. Online, SWYB combines model top-k candidates with automaton-proposed backup tokens, validates candidates through budgeted successor exploration, and uses the distance estimates for horizon-aware pruning and beam reranking. Any completed output returned by the decoder is guaranteed to be accepted by the target PDA.37:T47e,FFD combines content-aware scanning, a top-δ selection rule, and a fused selector-compute kernel. Instead of storing separate metadata such as centroids, partial-dimensional keys, or geometric bounds, it scans a compressed representation of the K cache itself. The K cache is decomposed into low-bit quantized thumbnails, used for fast query-key similarity estimation, plus a residual path for fidelity. The selection rule, top-δ, filters blocks according to their estimated contribution to the attention score sum. This differs from top-k, which imposes a fixed budget regardless of the attention entropy, and from top-p, which requires global probability accumulation. The paper argues that blocks whose contribution is below a numerically motivated threshold have negligible effect on the final attention output, and that the criterion can be approximately parallelized because LLM attention is often highly concentrated. At the systems level, FFD fuses scanning, selection, and attention computation into one kernel so that the compute phase reuses the selector’s intermediate estimates and avoids redundant HBM traffic and reduction bubbles.38:T6b6,The main idea is to decompose a standard MoE expert into composable internal sub-transformations and execute path compositions instead of whole experts. The paper builds on the common SwiGLU-style FFN expert used in models such as Mixtral and Qwen-MoE. In a vanilla expert, the input goes through parallel gate and up projections on the expansion side, then through element-wise gating, and finally through a down projection back to the hidden dimension. Standard MoE routing treats this entire computation as one atomic unit. PCoMoE instead turns it into a path-level execution space.

That creates a combinatorial problem: once internal components can be recombined, the number of possible paths can explode, which would hurt both quality and runtime. To control this, the paper introduces compatibility-aware gating and layer-wise pruning. Compatibility-aware gating suppresses low-value off-diagonal combinations, keeping only structurally plausible or useful path compositions. Layer-wise pruning further reduces the path space according to layer sensitivity, preserving more flexibility where the model is fragile and pruning more aggressively where redundancy is higher. Importantly, vanilla expert paths remain available, so the method augments rather than replaces the original execution graph.

The runtime design is a central part of the contribution. The authors propose a hardware-friendly execution engine that groups active paths by source and shares expansion-side operations, aiming to convert path-level flexibility into actual speedups instead of scheduling chaos. This system co-design is essential. Without it, the extra path freedom would likely be canceled out by dispatch and batching overhead.39:T4e5,From the provided full-text content, the main reported outcomes are end-to-end speedup and task accuracy. PCoMoE achieves up to 1.31x serving speedup, which is a meaningful gain if measured under realistic MoE serving conditions rather than isolated kernel benchmarks. The paper also claims up to 10% accuracy improvement over vanilla MoE baselines on downstream tasks. That number should be read carefully in the original tables, since it is likely task-specific or relative rather than a uniform absolute gain.

If you work on MoE inference or on designing experts that are easier to decompose and optimize, this is worth a quick read.3b:T7db,方法核心是 GLANCE。它不是再训练一个小型自回归 drafter，而是在冻结的目标 VLM 隐状态上加一个 one-pass block drafter。具体做法有三步。

第一步，使用 block-diffusion head 对一个长度为 B 的未来块同时建模。这里的关键不是把整个模型改成 diffusion LM，而是把 diffusion 式并行去噪/填充能力用作 speculative drafting head：给定当前已提交前缀和目标模型已经融合好的 vision-language hidden states，head 在一次前向里输出整个 block 各位置的分布。这样 depth 不再对应 k 次 sequential draft pass，而是一次 draft pass 就覆盖 k 个未来位置。

第二步，从整块分布中构造宽候选树。作者强调，在 one-pass drafting 的设定下，宽度比深度更便宜，因为整块已经算出来了，额外扩展多个高概率前缀主要把成本放在 verify 阶段，而不是重复 draft 阶段。于是 GLANCE 不是像传统 AR drafter 那样靠多轮逐步展开树，而是直接从 block 位置分布中提取高分前缀，形成 wide candidate tree。

第三步，用一次 target pass 验证整棵树，并证明最终提交路径与目标模型 greedy decoding 完全一致。这里的 lossless 条件很严格：不是近似一致，而是 bitwise equality with greedy decoding。作者还做了运行时 gating，不是假设等价，而是在每轮验证中检查提交路径是否满足精确一致条件。

论文还有一个很好的机制分析。作者提出 accepted block length 主要由 target 的 next-token entropy 决定，并在多个任务上拟合出统一规律。随后用 mismatched-image probe 证明图像的作用是通过降低条件熵进入系统：把图像换错，acceptance length 就按熵上升而下降；把 fused visual state 换成 text-only LLM 的状态，损失最大恰好出现在 grounded、低熵、原本最适合 speculative decoding 的任务上。这比“视觉信息有帮助”更具体，也更可操作。3c:T7f3,The method, GLANCE, replaces the usual small autoregressive drafter with a one-pass block drafter attached to the frozen target VLM’s hidden states. The design has three main pieces.

First, a block-diffusion head predicts a whole future block of length B in parallel. The key point is that the target model itself remains unchanged and autoregressive; the diffusion-style component is only the drafting head. Given the committed prefix and the target’s already fused vision-language state, the head outputs token distributions for all positions in the block in a single forward pass. This removes the usual depth cost of k sequential draft passes for k drafted tokens.

Second, GLANCE constructs a wide candidate tree from the block-level distributions. In this setup, width becomes the cheap axis because the block has already been drafted in one shot. Expanding multiple high-probability prefixes does not require repeated draft passes; most of the extra cost is pushed into verification. This is a major departure from standard autoregressive drafters, where both depth and width are expensive because they are built sequentially.

Third, the target verifies the whole tree in one pass, and the paper proves that the committed path is exactly identical to the target model’s own greedy decoding. The lossless claim is therefore strict: not approximate quality preservation, but exact equality to greedy output. The authors also add runtime gating so that equality is checked rather than assumed.

A particularly strong part of the paper is the mechanism analysis. The authors argue that accepted block length is governed by the target model’s next-token entropy, and they fit a single law across tasks. They then use a mismatched-image probe to show that the image helps through this entropy channel: replacing the image with a mismatched one raises uncertainty and shortens accepted blocks; replacing fused visual state with text-only hidden state hurts most on grounded tasks where acceptance should otherwise be longest.3d:T5ea,Three result groups matter most. First, end-to-end speedup: on grounded workloads such as document QA, infographic QA, and chart QA, GLANCE reaches up to 2.93× speedup over plain autoregressive decoding while preserving exact greedy outputs. One practical detail stands out: GLANCE uses one draft pass per round, whereas the production-style VLM EAGLE-3 head requires eight. Second, comparison against a strong baseline under matched training conditions: trained on the same corpus and schedule as an EAGLE-3 head, GLANCE achieves 2.7× longer accepted blocks. That suggests the gain comes from the one-pass block-drafting structure rather than from extra training budget. Third, mechanism validation: accepted length follows a common relationship with next-token entropy across tasks; grounded tasks sit at the low-entropy end and therefore accept the longest blocks, while open-ended description sits at the high-entropy end and accepts the shortest.

The paper also reports transfer of the acceptance law to a second VLM and to speech, code, and chat settings. If borne out in the full experiments, that makes the contribution more than a VLM-specific serving trick. Another interesting detail is the verbatim-copy analysis: on grounded tasks, measured acceptance can exceed the law’s nominal cap, which the authors attribute to long near-deterministic copy spans such as OCR-like generation. OCR-targeted retraining then increases acceptance in exactly the regions where the law predicts remaining headroom.3e:T57d,A good skim path is: diagnosis, method, law, deployment.
