第一部分是 Head-Local。Full-Head Mapping 的做法是：对每个目标层、目标 KV 头，从选定源层的所有源 KV 头拼接后做回归。作者认为这隐含了一个过强假设，即不同模型之间头的对应关系是全局稠密的。CacheBridge 改成 architecture-indexed 的局部支持：每个目标头只从一个源头块接收输入，但仍允许跨层聚合。这样做的直接效果是把每个目标头的 fan-in 从“所有源头”缩到“一个局部块”，系数数量按源头数成倍下降，文中是 8× 缩减。更重要的是，这个约束把映射偏置到更符合架构对应关系的子空间，减少了在架构差异较大时的错误耦合。

第二部分是 Attn-Repair。作者指出，传统 held-out R² 只衡量 cache 坐标重建，而生成质量取决于这些误差经过目标模型 query 与 attention 组合后的放大或抵消。因此相同的 KV 拟合误差，可能对应完全不同的续写漂移。Attn-Repair 的做法是按残差对接收模型 attention 输出的一阶影响来重加权，相当于让拟合更关注那些会真正改变后续注意力计算的方向，而不是平均对待所有 cache 坐标。为了避免权重过度集中到极少数样本，作者加入 effective-sample-size floor 来限制退化，但不改变在线映射形式。

第三部分是 Fused-Fit。由于不同目标层会选择不同源层支持，top-k layer 选择会造成碎片化 gather，通用拟合器在构建加权充分统计量时会反复做 scattered materialization、centering 和 weighting，内存流量很大。Fused-Fit 用新的 fused GPU kernel 在有界 panel 内直接构建 head-batched 矩阵乘法所需统计量，保持同样的 ridge solver 和同样的最终 mapper artifact，只是把离线构建过程做成结构感知的高效实现。这个部分没有改变数学目标，但大幅改善了 mapper construction 的时间和内存行为。

整体上，CacheBridge 不是提出新的在线推理协议，而是在“离线拟合、在线仿射应用”这个框架内，把支持结构、目标函数和实现路径都改得更贴近真实 continuation quality。40:T9b6,CacheBridge combines three components and keeps the online deployment interface unchanged: an offline-fitted affine mapper that can be applied directly at handoff time.

The first component is Head-Local. Full-Head Mapping regresses each target KV head on the concatenation of all source KV heads from selected source layers. CacheBridge argues that this assumes an overly dense correspondence between models. Instead, each target head is restricted to a single architecture-indexed source-head block, while still allowing cross-layer aggregation. This reduces fan-in dramatically and cuts the coefficient count by the number of source heads, 8× in the reported setup. More importantly, it biases the mapping toward a subspace that better matches architectural locality, reducing harmful cross-head coupling when the source and target architectures differ.

The second component is Attn-Repair. The paper points out that held-out R² only measures coordinate-wise cache reconstruction, while continuation quality depends on how those errors propagate through the target model’s queries and attention computation. Two mappings with similar cache fit can therefore produce very different continuation drift. Attn-Repair reweights residuals according to their first-order effect on the receiver’s attention output. In other words, it emphasizes errors that actually matter for downstream attention behavior rather than treating all cache coordinates equally. An effective-sample-size floor prevents the weighting from collapsing onto a tiny subset of examples, while preserving the same online affine form.

The third component is Fused-Fit. Because different target layers may choose different source-layer supports, top-k support selection creates fragmented gather patterns. A generic fitter repeatedly materializes scattered tensors, centers them, and applies weights, so memory traffic becomes a major cost. Fused-Fit introduces a fused GPU kernel that constructs the weighted sufficient statistics directly in bounded panels for head-batched matrix multiplication. It does not change the ridge objective, the solver, or the deployed mapper artifact; it simply makes offline construction structure-aware and much more efficient.

Taken together, CacheBridge does not propose a new online protocol. It refines the existing offline-fit / online-affine-transfer framework by redesigning support structure, fitting objective, and construction path around actual continuation quality.41:T70b,The evaluation covers three transfer directions, with two difficult Ministral 3 directions and one Qwen3 direction being the most informative. The paper first uses Full-Head Mapping to expose model sensitivity. Under the same 500-sequence calibration protocol and the same 8×128 KV interface, transfer to Qwen3 32B remains close to the target baseline, 79.2% versus 80.2%. But the two Ministral 3 directions targeting 14B drop sharply to 52.2% and 44.4%. This shows that the existence of a linear transfer path does not mean dense all-head mapping is the right inductive bias.

CacheBridge recovers 20.4 and 31.6 HellaSwag points on those two difficult directions, while preserving 99.83% mean target retention on Qwen3 14B→32B. So the gain is not coming from overfitting to one architecture family. On efficiency, mapper storage on Qwen3 drops from 4.296 GB to 0.538 GB, roughly an 8× reduction, and online application is up to 3.0× faster. For offline construction, the median time to build the 500-sequence Qwen3 mapper is 8.63 seconds in the reported setup.

The paper also analyzes three important phenomena. First, application latency grows almost linearly with the number of supported source layers k; on Ministral 3B→14B, transfer approaches target-side re-prefill by k=16 and exceeds it from k=20 onward. That means uncontrolled support growth can erase the systems benefit of cache transfer. Second, KV fit and continuation quality are misaligned: similar R² can correspond to very different attention drift. Third, top-k support causes fragmented construction, which is exactly the bottleneck Fused-Fit addresses. The most useful aspect of the experiments is that they optimize quality, online cost, and offline construction cost together rather than reporting only transfer accuracy.42:T7d1,REAL-Q changes both the objective and the solver.

On the objective side, it replaces the standard layer-local reconstruction MSE with an end-to-end-aligned surrogate called Aggregated Fisher MSE. This surrogate is derived from a second-order Taylor expansion of the global KL divergence at the current transformer block output. Unlike grouped approximations that discard cross-channel interactions, REAL-Q keeps the full aggregated Fisher matrix, so output-channel coupling is preserved. To keep the computation manageable, the expansion point is chosen so that backpropagation only needs to traverse at most two adjacent blocks rather than the full network. The method also introduces a loss sliding window to smooth transitions across neighboring blocks, reducing discontinuities in the optimization landscape during sequential block-wise quantization.

On the optimization side, the paper argues that the core limitation of the GPTQ lineage is its dependence on a closed-form column-wise solver. That requirement forces heavy Hessian compression and then freezes the approximation for the whole layer. REAL-Q instead uses Dynamic Block-wise Gradient Descent. It still follows a sequential column-wise quantization pipeline, but after each column block of 128 columns it inserts one Adam update. The gradient is recomputed online against the actual partially quantized model state, so the method can correct accumulated upstream errors and adapt to the shifted loss landscape as quantization progresses. The authors describe this as increasing the correction granularity from per-layer to per-column-block, roughly two orders of magnitude finer. Adam’s diagonal preconditioning provides an implicit second-order effect without explicit Hessian inversion.

Importantly, REAL-Q is not a complete departure from GPTQ-style pipelines. It is a practical modification that keeps the sequential structure while making both the loss and the correction mechanism more faithful to the end-to-end objective.43:T45e,The experiments cover LLaMA-3.1 8B and 70B, and Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B. The main metric is KL divergence under weight-only W4A16 quantization, compared against GPTQ and more recent variants. The headline result is that REAL-Q achieves the lowest KL on every evaluated model, with up to about 49% KL reduction on Qwen3-1.7B at W4A16.

That result supports two claims: the end-to-end-aligned Fisher-based objective is better than plain layer-local reconstruction loss, and dynamic online updates help mitigate the error accumulation that appears in sequential quantization.

The most important ablations are likely the contribution of Aggregated Fisher MSE over standard reconstruction losses, the effect of the loss sliding window on stability across block boundaries, and the role of Block-GD frequency and optimizer choice. The excerpt does not include the full numeric tables, but those ablations are where the paper’s argument really stands or falls. In particular, the key question is whether the gain mainly comes from a better loss, from more frequent online correction, or from the combination of both.44:T436,For a skim, start with the introduction and read the critique of GPTQ-style methods carefully. The three failure modes to keep in mind are uncorrected upstream perturbations, poor modeling of downstream sensitivity, and frozen second-order information inside a layer. Then move to the method overview and the derivation of Aggregated Fisher MSE, followed by the Block-GD algorithm. The main thing to understand is why the backpropagation can stay local to nearby blocks and why updating every 128 columns is a practical compromise.

In the results, prioritize the main comparison table and the ablations. The main table answers whether the method wins consistently; the ablations explain why. A useful skim should take about 25 to 35 minutes. For deeper reading, check the appendix for complexity analysis, calibration-data details, and whether gains are consistent across model scales. Another important question is whether lower KL translates into better perplexity or generation quality in deployment, since that determines the practical meaning of the reported improvements.45:T7a9,The key idea is not to exempt important weights from quantization, but to quantize all weights into a compact ternary base first and then spend a small residual budget where ternary quantization hurts the most. In the sub-2-bit regime, this is a more efficient use of bits than simply bypassing quantization for selected weights.

The method has three main components.

First, a ternary base representation. Following PT2-LLM-style formulations, each quantization group uses a scale α and bias β, and weights are mapped to one of three values: {β-α, β, β+α}. This gives a compact ternary approximation for all weights.

Second, a salient residual design called column-semi sparse salient weight. QTEA first selects important columns, then keeps only a sparse subset of high-impact entries within those columns under a 1:4 semi-structured sparsity pattern. These retained entries act as residual corrections to the ternary base. This is a useful compromise: more regular than unstructured salient-weight preservation, but more bit-efficient than storing full salient columns.

Third, the paper modifies GPTQ-style column-by-column quantization in two ways. It adds column-wise rescale refinement, which alternates between updating a per-column rescale factor and the ternary assignment so that the ternary base better matches the local weight distribution after Hessian-aware error propagation. It also introduces error decay. The motivation is that GPTQ’s error propagation is order-dependent: early columns can spread their error over many later columns, while late columns have little room left, so using the same propagation strength everywhere can overcompensate near the end. Error decay gradually weakens propagation along the column order to reduce this imbalance.

Overall, QTEA is a combination of ternary base quantization, structured residual compensation, and a refined column-wise optimization procedure tailored to ultra-low-bit settings.46:T5c7,The main experiments are on Qwen3-14B and Llama3-8B. On Qwen3-14B, QTEA improves average downstream-task accuracy by 16.7% over the strongest ternary PTQ baseline reported by the authors, while reducing perplexity by 1.40× on WikiText and 2.61× on C4. On Llama3-8B, it improves average downstream accuracy by 6.6% and reduces perplexity by 1.34× on WikiText and 1.95× on C4. The larger gain on Qwen3-14B suggests the method remains useful across model families and may be especially helpful where ternary quantization is more brittle.

The paper also reports a better size-versus-perplexity trade-off on Qwen3, which supports the claim that the residual budget is being allocated more effectively.

On the systems side, the authors implement dedicated CUDA kernels and combine them with CUDA Graphs. They report up to 7.2× generation speedup over an FP16 baseline with CUDA Graphs, and up to 13.3× over FP16 without CUDA Graphs. These numbers should be interpreted carefully because the gain comes from both quantization and systems optimization, but the paper does close the loop between representation design and practical inference speed.

The most important ablations to inspect are likely the contribution of the residual representation, the effect of column-wise rescale refinement, and the effect of error decay on late-column instability. The provided text does not include all ablation numbers, but those are the components most directly tied to the claimed gains.47:T465,Start with the introduction. It clearly explains why low-batch decoding is bandwidth-bound, why sub-2-bit PTQ is difficult, and what existing salient-weight methods give up. Then read the Quantized Ternary Error Adaptation section carefully. Focus on three pieces: the ternary base definition, the column-semi sparse residual structure, and where rescale refinement and error decay enter the GPTQ-style pipeline.

If the goal is a quick assessment, prioritize two kinds of results: model-quality comparisons across more than one backbone, and throughput/kernel results that validate the hardware-friendly design. That is enough to judge whether the method is only an offline quantization trick or something deployable.

A 20–30 minute read should cover the main idea. For deeper study, inspect the explanation of order-dependent overcompensation in late columns and the appendix sections on kernel implementation. For pretraining-oriented readers, the most transferable lesson is not the quantization formula itself, but how the paper decomposes error into representation, optimization-order, and hardware-structure issues.48:T87d,文章延续前作的“integer alibi”思路，但这次把论证做成了可操作的测量。

第一步是 fault injection。作者构造了一个 W8A8 参考实现，其中 INT8×INT8 到 INT32 的 accumulator 按设计是精确的，因此任何跨实现差异都只能来自 epilogue。然后他们从 Qwen3-1.7B 的 196 个捕获层中回放真实操作数，在这个参考流水线上注入 9 类 fault，形成一个预先定义的 check–fault 矩阵。最初是 63 个 cell，经过一个公开的两层 smoke run 后扩展到 77 个 cell，并只修正了 3 个预测，再锁定协议跑完整实验。这个预注册式设计的好处是，避免“看完结果再设计 fault”的自我强化。

第二步是分析为什么 tolerance-based conformance 会失效。作者的论点很清楚：对于 epilogue 中的 rounding mode 或中间精度差异，输出一旦变化，通常只会落到相邻的一个可表示 bfloat16 值上，也就是最多偏移一个 bfloat16 spacing；而一个 spacing 已经是允许合法浮点差异的最小容差。于是“合法实现差异”和“错误实现差异”落在同一个容差区间里，任何基于 tolerance 的检查都无法把两者分开。这不是阈值没调好，而是可分性不存在。

第三步是提出可部署的 power-of-two scale 方案。前作曾用 power-of-two scales 作为诊断探针，能恢复 bitwise 一致性，但 perplexity 恶化了 +157%，因此当时不能作为实际方案。本文指出那个结果是因为只改写了存储的 scales，却没有重新量化权重，属于 operand mismatch fault。作者这次做的是 requantized power-of-two checkpoints：把 scale 约束为 2 的幂，并重新量化权重，使 epilogue 的 scale 乘法变成精确的指数调整，从而消除 kernel 之间在浮点乘法与舍入路径上的自由度。这样，唯一真正严格的 bitwise check 才有可服务的 checkpoint 可用。

第四步是把 conformance suite 的能力边界讲清楚。结果不是“suite 很强”，而是“suite 在某些 fault 上完全无能为力”。这点写得比较诚实，也比单纯展示零误报更有价值。49:T915,The work extends the earlier “integer alibi” argument but turns it into a careful measurement study.

First, the authors build a fault-injection setup. They use a reference W8A8 pipeline in which the INT8×INT8 to INT32 accumulation is exact by construction, so any disagreement must come from the epilogue. They replay operands captured from 196 layers of Qwen3-1.7B and inject nine fault families with known ground truth. This yields a pre-specified check–fault matrix: initially 63 cells, then expanded to 77 after a disclosed two-layer smoke run that corrected only three predictions before the full run. That pre-registered structure matters because it prevents the suite from being evaluated only on faults it was implicitly designed to catch.

Second, the paper explains why tolerance-based conformance fails for epilogue behavior. If the fault is a rounding-mode change or an intermediate-precision change, the output, when it changes at all, typically moves to a neighboring representable bfloat16 value—at most one bfloat16 spacing. But one spacing is already the smallest tolerance that still admits legal floating-point differences across correct implementations. So legal variation and faulty variation overlap exactly where a tolerance check must operate. The limitation is structural, not a matter of choosing a better epsilon.

Third, the paper revisits power-of-two scales as a deployable mitigation. The companion paper had shown that power-of-two scales restore bitwise agreement, but the reported perplexity degradation was +157%, making the idea unusable in practice. This paper shows that the earlier degradation came from rewriting stored scales without requantizing the weights, which is itself an operand-mismatch fault. The new setup uses requantized power-of-two checkpoints: scales are constrained to powers of two and weights are requantized accordingly, so the epilogue becomes an exactly checkable exponent adjustment rather than a free floating-point multiply-and-round path.

Fourth, the paper is explicit about the limits of the conformance suite. The result is not “the suite works well everywhere,” but rather “the suite is exact where it applies and blind where tolerance cannot separate legal from faulty behavior.” That honesty is one of the stronger parts of the paper.4a:T57f,There are two main experimental takeaways.

The first is the sensitivity study of the conformance suite. Against the corrected 77-cell prediction matrix, the suite achieves zero false positives and zero false negatives. But this is not the comforting result it might first appear to be. Four of the five epilogue fault classes are not caught by any check in any of their 4,704 cells. That is a strong negative result: the blind spot is systematic, not anecdotal. The explanation is the one-bfloat16-spacing overlap between legal and faulty outputs.

The second is the quality cost of power-of-two scales. The earlier +157% perplexity increase is shown to be an artifact of a bad probe construction—rewriting scales without requantizing weights. With proper requantization, the observed perplexity point estimates across three model sizes fall between -0.28% and +0.48%, while the two kernels become byte-for-byte identical. That changes the status of power-of-two scales from a diagnostic trick to a plausible deployment option.

On the setup side, using operands replayed from 196 captured layers of Qwen3-1.7B makes the fault study more realistic than purely synthetic tests. The paper also emphasizes its pre-registered protocol and append-only amendments: the fault catalogue, thresholds, and analysis rules were fixed before the main run, with only limited corrections after the disclosed smoke test.4b:T49c,The intervention is deliberately minimal. Using Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, the authors intercept the complete visual interface produced by the vision module: the main visual-token tensor X_main plus K=3 DeepStack feature streams X_DS,k. Each tensor is independently passed through an NNC encode→decode round trip, and the reconstructed tensors replace the originals before LLM decoding continues. Everything else is frozen (weights, prompts, tokenizer, decoding), so any output change is attributable to interface compression.
Key choices:
- Evaluate compression by downstream task metrics rather than reconstruction fidelity; representation-level distortion is analyzed but treated as a weak proxy for utility.
- Use a single shared QP (quantization parameter) across all streams to sweep rate vs task performance.
- Include two bounding controls: Identity (no compression) and Zero-token (replace interface with zeros) to bracket the useful operating regime.
- Keep codec configuration fixed (uniform approximation, dependent quantization, row skipping enabled; quantize-only mode; TCA disabled; sparsity 0.0), varying only QP to avoid confounding from codec hyperparameter tuning.4c:T449,Setup: Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct in BF16, batch size 1. Benchmarks:
- Video-MME (closed-ended): parse model output into an option letter; report strict accuracy and a separate valid-rate (parseability) to disentangle formatting failures from reasoning failures.
- MLVU summary subset (open-ended): scored by a GPT-4 judge on completeness and reliability (0–5 each, summed to 10).
- 100 deterministically selected test samples per benchmark (skipping unresolved video files).
Compression rate is measured against the aggregate BF16 size of the full visual interface (main tokens + all DeepStack streams).
Only a partial numeric point is visible in the provided excerpt (e.g., 58.4% relative size at a certain QP; the remainder is truncated). The main reported behavior is: bitrate decreases monotonically with QP; task accuracy stays close to the uncompressed baseline under fairly aggressive compression until a sharp degradation region; reconstructions are heavily discretized/distorted yet remain usable for the decoder, supporting the claim that exact floating-point reconstruction is unnecessary.4d:T61c,There are two main components. First is dataset construction. Instead of scraping noisy online conversations or using lightly controlled crowdworkers, the authors hire professional script writers to produce complete human-to-human dialogues. The tasks are goal-directed but open-ended, such as tutoring, planning, or everyday assistance. They intentionally avoid heavy knowledge retrieval, coding, or tasks with a single correct endpoint. That design choice matters: if the task is too knowledge-bound, the benchmark becomes another factual QA test; if it is too rigidly task-scripted, it stops measuring natural conversation.

Second is annotation and metric analysis. UPHELD provides dense turn-level labels rather than only conversation-level scores. The labels target dimensions such as stylistic consistency, content consistency, and coherence. This lets the benchmark expose local failures inside a long interaction instead of averaging them away. The paper then compares several evaluation families: classical lexical/semantic metrics, single LLM-as-a-judge systems, and a learned mixture-of-judges built using UPHELD supervision. The main takeaway is that standard metrics and single judges correlate poorly with human judgments on realistic dialogue, especially for long-range conversational properties, while a simple learned ensemble tracks humans better. The interesting contribution is less the ensemble itself and more the empirical demonstration that synthetic-data-based judge validation does not transfer cleanly to real human-scale conversations.4e:T46f,The most important results are about dataset scale, distribution, and metric validity. UPHELD contains hundreds of complete dialogues, more than 30,000 human-written turns, and 153,578 dense turn-level human labels. The authors position this as roughly an order-of-magnitude increase over comparable human-verified dialogue evaluation resources. They also analyze dialogue length distributions and argue that realistic human task-oriented conversations are usually much shorter than many benchmark setups; they cite an average of about 9.3 turns in fully human-collected datasets, with Topical-Chat maxing out at 21 turns, and allow writers to stop naturally rather than forcing long transcripts. On evaluation, traditional NLP metrics and single LLM judges show weak correlation with human ratings on UPHELD, especially on style and content consistency, while the learned mixture-of-judges improves correlation. The excerpt does not expose the full numeric table, but the paper’s claim is that the gains are consistent across settings. The error analysis also emphasizes failures caused by synthetic dialogue bias and judge leakage.4f:T5d4,MemToC is built as a controlled post-tool-call benchmark derived from ToolHop.
- Data pipeline: start from ToolHop sub-questions with locally executable tool calls and verified intermediate answers; keep only self-contained facts with short verifiable answers.
- Pre-construct benchmark artifacts before evaluating any model: question q, verified gold g, executable call, and curated distractors to synthesize plausible incorrect tool returns. Two annotators independently review for self-containedness, answer leakage, answer validity, and distractor plausibility.
- For each model and each prompt wording variant, first elicit a closed-book answer m (forced to answer, no abstention) and score it against g to determine whether the model’s memory is correct.
- Then present the same question with an injected tool return r under four conditions: correct return, incorrect return (built from verified answers and human-validated distractors), error payload, and no return. Because r is injected, tool correctness is known a priori.
- This yields a source-correctness matrix where the “correct behavior” is well-defined (use correct tools, resist incorrect tools), with tool-error/no-tool as controls.
- Evaluation details include extraction-first answer matching and three instruction-wording variants with fixed question text.
- Mitigations: compare prompting vs SFT vs DPO, using cross-fitting over ToolHop chains so that each reported fine-tuned prediction is on held-out questions.50:T525,The benchmark is organized around two aligned axes. On the math side, the authors define a taxonomy of atomic capabilities in three levels: Level 1 covers foundational concepts and calculation, including symbol recognition, concept understanding, and calculation; Level 2 covers advanced reasoning and application, including spatial perception, formalization, deductive and inductive reasoning, and mathematical modeling; Level 3 covers meta-cognition, including theorem application, self-reflection, and new knowledge learning. On the agent side, these are aligned with Planning, Action, and Feedback. The key point is that the benchmark evaluates the intersection rather than simply relabeling math skills: planning is framed as capability selection, ordering, and next-step decision making; action as isolated execution of a single atomic capability; feedback as monitoring and revising an existing trajectory. The dataset construction uses an automated pipeline with data collection, trajectory synthesis, multi-stage filtering, and fine-grained annotation, and it includes both text-only and multimodal settings. A notable design choice is to decouple intrinsic agentic evaluation from full agent deployment, so the benchmark measures reusable process capabilities without requiring a complete tool-using system.51:T4e0,1) Task formulation (VTEC): split into Error Detection (locate wrong tokens/regions) and Error Correction (produce the corrected text), with samples designed to be unsolvable from linguistic context alone.
2) High-quality test set: manually curated real-world images with natural errors; strict selection rule that visual cues are necessary; multi-stage annotation with cross-checking and adjudication; plus error-free images from EST-VQA/TextVQA for detection calibration. Final test set size: 1,229.
3) Scalable training set for targeted training/RL: a three-stage Generate–Edit–Examination pipeline.
- Generate: GPT-4o proposes corrupted text; Qwen3-235B filters out cases fixable by language-only reasoning.
- Edit: Qwen-Image-Edit-2509 writes the corrupted text back into the image regions.
- Examination: Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct performs correction/verification to filter low-quality edits and label mismatches.

4) Evaluation paradigms: (a) prompt-based strategies (direct correction, background information enhancement), and (b) targeted model training including RL-based tuning, aiming to approximate each model’s ceiling before concluding there remains a large human gap.52:T5eb,FaithSieve has three stages: localization, verification, and synthesis. In localization, the system decomposes coarse benchmark steps into finer EdgeUnits using a proof-state-tree representation. Each transition in this tree corresponds to a local reasoning responsibility, which makes the evaluation target much sharper than judging an entire paragraph-like step. In verification, the method extracts typed proof obligations from suspicious transitions. These obligations are not treated uniformly; they encode different kinds of reasoning responsibilities such as algebraic transformation, implication transfer, existence construction, boundary-condition handling, or case transitions. The system then gathers evidence through both lightweight checks and Lean-based validation. Lean is used as a structured evidence source rather than a direct judge. A key safeguard is the semantic alignment score, which measures whether the formalized statement preserves the assumptions, directionality, quantification, and strength of the original informal obligation. Lean evidence is only trusted when this alignment is high enough, preventing drifted or weakened targets from producing false reassurance. In synthesis, local evidence is aggregated back to the original step level to predict the first erroneous benchmark step. The main novelty is the full pipeline: decomposition into local transitions, typed obligations, formal checking gated by semantic alignment, and evidence aggregation for first-error localization.53:T506,The paper introduces two expert-verified datasets: ProofLoc-Olympiad with 350 algebra and number theory problems, and ProofLoc-University with 200 advanced mathematics problems. On ProofLoc-Olympiad, FaithSieve reaches 81.43% exact first-error accuracy, compared with 72.29% for a GPT-5.4 direct-judging baseline, an absolute gain of 9.14 points. The provided text also states that FaithSieve shows clear gains on ProofLoc-University, although the exact number is not visible in the excerpt. The evaluation follows the standard first-error localization setup, reporting both binary accuracy and exact accuracy, with the latter requiring the correct first-error index. The experimental story is important because it tests whether local formal evidence, when filtered for semantic faithfulness, actually improves early-error localization. The likely key ablations are removing EdgeUnit decomposition, which should make local flaws harder to isolate; removing semantic alignment gating, which should increase false positives from target drift; and relying only on natural-language judging, which should weaken precise localization. Together these results support a narrow but important claim: formal verification helps only when the verified target is both local and semantically faithful.54:T75e,The benchmark construction pipeline is graph-based and deliberately audit-friendly. The corpus is first partitioned by a quality classifier into D_high and D_low. Instead of mining the retained high-quality pool, the authors search D_low for low-exposure facts that are more likely to reveal parametric memory limits. Documents in D_low become nodes in a graph. Support edges connect documents about the same specific fact, while conflict edges connect documents that give incompatible accounts for the same subject-attribute pair.

A naive all-pairs comparison would be quadratic, so the paper uses a two-stage narrowing strategy. First, an LLM assigns each document a knowledge-point label, and candidate comparisons are restricted within those clusters. Second, entity-based retrieval further reduces the candidate set. Only then are LLM judgments used to verify support and conflict relations. This is an important design choice: the LLM is used offline to structure the corpus and identify disagreements, not to provide evidence at evaluation time.

Verified conflict edges seed subgraph sampling and QA synthesis. Each question is paired with an answer set containing at least two verified accounts, and every answer must remain traceable to source documents, externally checked against authoritative public sources, and reviewed by human annotators. The evaluation is closed-book: no retrieval, no source passages, no tools.

The metric design is also central. The paper separates fact recall from account completeness. A model may recover one account and therefore show some memory of the fact, yet still fail the completeness criterion by omitting the alternative verified account. The authors then use the number of supporting documents on each side of a disagreement as an exposure proxy, which allows them to analyze how corpus prevalence relates to these two failure modes.55:T58e,ElephantBench contains 1,094 closed-book questions mined from naturally occurring disagreements in a low-exposure web corpus. Each item is source-traceable, externally verified, and human-reviewed. The evaluation covers 32 models. The headline result is that even the strongest model recovers both accounts on only 52.4% of questions. On nearly all of the remaining cases, the model does not fail by total ignorance; instead, it recalls one verified account while omitting the other. That makes incompleteness, not pure forgetting, the dominant error mode.

The most informative analysis is the exposure asymmetry study. By counting how many documents support each side of a disagreement, the paper approximates relative corpus exposure. The more prevalent account is more predictive of whether the model recalls the fact at all. The less prevalent account is more predictive of whether the model recalls the full set of verified accounts. This is a clean empirical link between corpus imbalance and partial memory retention.

The paper also argues for construction efficiency. Knowledge-point clustering and entity-based retrieval reduce the need for exhaustive pairwise LLM judging. The excerpt provided here does not include the full cost table, but the design goal is clear: make the pipeline reusable for turning any low-exposure corpus into a memory probe rather than building a one-off benchmark by manual curation.56:T47b,Start with the introduction and benchmark positioning. The key is to see why this is neither a standard long-tail QA benchmark nor a standard conflict-reasoning benchmark. Then read the pipeline section around Figure 2 carefully. D_low, the document graph, support versus conflict edges, and the QA synthesis process are the structural core of the work.

After that, focus on the metric definitions and the exposure analysis. The paper becomes much more interesting once you see that it is not just making QA harder; it is separating recall from completeness and tying both to corpus prevalence. That is the part most relevant to pretraining data decisions.

If reading time is limited, prioritize: the task definition, the graph construction figure, the main results table with the 52.4% complete-recall ceiling, and the plots analyzing support-document asymmetry. For a deeper read, inspect the human review protocol, external verification criteria, and how conflict-edge precision is controlled, because benchmark noise will matter a lot for interpreting the memory-completeness claim.57:T5c5,CURA is a read-only external monitor. It observes harness-visible telemetry rather than hidden states, logits, or internal traces. The monitored system is a three-stage pipeline: a read-only feasibility gate, a planner, and a GUI executor. CURA converts the trajectory into a sequential risk process built from four families of task-agnostic signals: execution effort, reasoning semantics, execution physiology, and visual dynamics. Intuitively, these capture how much work the agent is doing, what kind of reasoning it is expressing, whether its action rhythm looks unhealthy, and whether the screen is changing in ways consistent with progress. The online detector is based on CUSUM, which accumulates evidence over time instead of making a one-shot judgment. Thresholds are calibrated with Learn-then-Test using successful trajectories only, yielding finite-sample false-alarm guarantees without requiring failure labels. This design choice is important: the goal is not to maximize retrospective AUROC, but to detect failure early under a controlled false-alarm budget. The paper also studies where signal enters the pipeline: some risk is measurable before the first action, more appears at the planning stage, but fast quiet failures and belief-level errors remain difficult for purely external monitoring. The authors further test common alternatives such as token-level log-probability confidence and single-screenshot LLM judging, and find them weak on this benchmark.58:T54e,Experiments are run on 361 OSWorld-Verified tasks. The monitored pipeline achieves a mean task score of 82.9 and a full-solve rate of 80.3% (290/361), above the human reference of 72.4 reported in the paper. The central empirical finding is the oversight gap: among 71 failures, 64 (90%) still end with a success claim; 61 of those 64 acknowledge no blocker; and the explicit failure affordance is never used in roughly 9,100 executor calls. As a retrospective baseline, token count is already strong at 0.802 AUROC, while CURA’s composite reaches 0.828, not a large offline separation. The online story is more favorable. Under matched false-alarm budgets, CURA detects more failures: at α=0.10, recall is 0.41 versus 0.34 for token-count triggers; at α=0.20, 0.56 versus 0.38. The paper also reports that at α=0.10, CURA detects 42.3% of failures a median of 31 steps before termination with a realized false-alarm rate of 0.066. When alarms are used to route trajectories to a stronger overseer, 23 of 70 failures are recovered while escalating only 38 trajectories, producing a cascade with mean task score 86.8 and full-solve rate 84.5%. Early-stage predictability is also quantified: gate-probe telemetry reaches 0.69 AUROC and plan-stage evidence 0.74.59:T713,方法上，作者把问题形式化成 call-decision test。每个样本先有 ASR transcript，再由 text LLM 给出 transcript-side label；同时系统还可以选择调用本地音频 encoder（CLAP、AST、WavLM）或 generative audio model（Qwen2-Audio、Qwen2.5-Omni、MOSS-Audio）。关键不是单独比较这些模型，而是训练一个 routing / selection policy，在固定开发集上决定何时保留 transcript 标签、何时看 encoder、何时发起 generative call。

论文设计了几种策略。transcript-first route 用 transcript 风险分数来决定是否升级到 generative model；风险分数由 transcript label 的开发集错误率估计、Whisper 不确定性、text-LLM label likelihood 不确定性、以及是否输出非法标签等特征组成。encoder-first route 则先让 CLAP 对所有波形打分，再把低 margin 样本送去 generative model。更强的 full selector 把问题写成 row-action 对上的 correctness prediction：用 L2 正则 logistic model 预测某个动作在某个样本上是否会答对，特征包括动作置信度、transcript 不确定性和长度、encoder/generative 标记、动作成本、动作身份等。CLAP 和 WavLM 的开发集预测采用 out-of-fold，避免 selector 直接吃到泄漏的监督信号。

最关键的对照是 matched no-call selector。它和 full selector 使用同样的训练协议、同样的开发集调参流程，只是把 generative actions 整体移除。这样 full-vs-no-call 的差异就能更干净地解释成“生成式音频调用本身的边际价值”，而不是 selector 更强、特征更多、或调参更充分。作者还把成本单独报告，不把 latency / privacy / hosted exposure 混进 accuracy 里。这个设计很工整，适合做接口层面的审计。5a:T66a,主实验在 Dynamic-SUPERB VocalSound 六分类任务上进行，chance 为 0.167。开发集 480 条，holdout 240 条，并做了文件 stem、推测 speaker/session 等层面的无重叠检查。这个任务先验证 transcript 不够用：transcript-only 只有 0.296 accuracy。直接看音频模型时，Qwen2.5-Omni 达到 0.883，Qwen2-Audio 0.838，MOSS-Audio 0.808，zero-shot CLAP 0.762，AudioSet AST 0.404。到这里如果停下，很容易得出“必须用 generative audio model”的结论。

但作者继续加入开发集监督的 encoder 控制组，结论就变了。CLAP class-bias tuning 到 0.792；CLAP score probe 0.796 accuracy / 0.784 macro-F1；CLAP embedding probe 0.850 / 0.849；AST embedding probe 0.817 / 0.813；WavLM-base+ probe 0.854 / 0.853。再往上，CLAP–WavLM correctness oracle 到 0.938，联合 CLAP–WavLM ridge probe 到 0.896 / 0.892。也就是说，在这个闭集任务上，轻量或中等规模的判别式音频表示已经吃掉了 generative audio model 的大部分收益空间。

摘要给出的 headline 结论更直接：在 VocalSound 上，supervised selector 在 full action set 下达到 0.900 accuracy，而去掉所有 generative actions 的 matched no-call selector 仍有 0.892，差值只有 0.008，且 95% bootstrap CI 为 [-0.025, 0.042]。这说明在已知标签决策里，生成式音频调用的边际收益很小。作者还在 ESC-50 Animals、AudioBench 的情感子集、以及 SpeechTextMatching 上做了补充实验，用来说明这个结论的适用范围是“known closed-set label decisions”，而不是开放式对话或一般音频推理。5b:T6cc,The task is framed as a call-decision problem. For each example, the system has an ASR transcript, a transcript-side label from a text LLM, optional local audio encoders such as CLAP, AST, and WavLM, and optional generative audio models such as Qwen2-Audio, Qwen2.5-Omni, and MOSS-Audio. The goal is not to compare these components in isolation, but to learn a policy that decides when to keep the transcript label, when to rely on encoder evidence, and when to make a generative audio call.

Several routing strategies are evaluated. A transcript-first route uses a transcript risk score built from development-estimated transcript error risk, normalized Whisper uncertainty, text-LLM label-likelihood uncertainty, and an invalid-label flag. An encoder-first route uses CLAP margins and sends low-confidence cases to a generative model. The strongest setup is a full selector: an L2-regularized logistic correctness model over row-action pairs, with features including action confidence, transcript uncertainty and length, encoder flags, generative-call flags, action cost, and action identity. CLAP and WavLM development predictions are generated out-of-fold to avoid leakage.

The decisive control is the matched no-call selector. It uses the same training protocol, the same development tuning procedure, and the same selection machinery, but removes all generative actions. That makes the full-versus-no-call comparison a clean estimate of the marginal value of generative audio calls, rather than a comparison confounded by different selectors or different tuning effort. Costs are reported separately from accuracy, which keeps latency, privacy exposure, and hosted-interface concerns from being folded into the main accuracy metric.5c:T6f7,The main benchmark is Dynamic-SUPERB VocalSound, a six-way human-vocalization classification task with chance accuracy 0.167. The development split has 480 rows and the holdout has 240, with checks for overlap in file stems and inferred speaker/session groupings. The first result confirms that transcripts are insufficient: transcript-only accuracy is 0.296. Audio models are much stronger: Qwen2.5-Omni reaches 0.883, Qwen2-Audio 0.838, MOSS-Audio 0.808, zero-shot CLAP 0.762, and AudioSet AST 0.404. If evaluation stopped there, one could easily conclude that generative audio models are necessary.

The more informative comparison comes after adding supervised encoder controls. CLAP class-bias tuning reaches 0.792. A CLAP score probe reaches 0.796 accuracy and 0.784 macro-F1. A CLAP embedding probe reaches 0.850 and 0.849. AST embeddings reach 0.817 and 0.813. A WavLM-base+ probe reaches 0.854 and 0.853. A CLAP-WavLM correctness oracle reaches 0.938, and a joint CLAP-WavLM ridge probe reaches 0.896 and 0.892. These results show that discriminative audio representations already recover most of the benefit on this closed-set task.

The headline result from the abstract is the key one: on VocalSound, the supervised selector with the full action set reaches 0.900 accuracy, while the matched no-call selector still reaches 0.892. The gap is only 0.008, with a 95% bootstrap interval of [-0.025, 0.042]. In other words, once transcript and encoder evidence are available to the same development-selected policy, generative audio calls add little on this task. Additional experiments on ESC-50 Animals, an AudioBench emotion subset, and SpeechTextMatching are used to bound the claim to known closed-set label decisions rather than open dialogue or general audio reasoning.5d:T4f9,Read the introduction with the scope restriction in mind. The paper is not arguing against audio-LLMs in general. It is asking whether generative calls are justified for known closed-set decisions. Then go straight to the Generative-Call Decision Test section. The relationship between the full selector and the matched no-call selector is the methodological center of the paper.

After that, inspect the main VocalSound table and the call-rate frontier. Keep the two comparisons separate: transcript-only versus audio evidence tells you whether acoustics matter; full selector versus no-call selector tells you whether generative calls have marginal value once other evidence is available. Confusing these two is exactly the evaluation mistake the paper is trying to correct.

If time is short, prioritize the task formulation, the selector design, the main VocalSound results, the paired intervals for full versus no-call, and the cost definition. Around 20 to 30 minutes should be enough for a solid skim. For a deeper read, check the 10-seed selector stability analysis, the Holm-adjusted testing protocol, and the discussion of why Qwen2 and Omni lack comparable token-level confidence traces, since that affects how fairly the selector can exploit generative outputs.5e:T475,The benchmark combines four visually grounded datasets: ClockQA for analog clock reading, PathVQA for pathology images, MathVision for mathematical reasoning over figures, and SB-Bench for demographic and stereotype-related visual reasoning. Each item is paired with an intentionally wrong user answer. For multiple-choice tasks, the wrong answer is sampled from incorrect options; for PathVQA, it is the inverse of the ground truth; for ClockQA, it is produced by perturbing the correct time. The evaluation covers single-turn and multi-turn pressure, five pressure conditions, and five LMRMs: GPT-5.4-Mini, Claude-Sonnet-4.6, Gemini-3-Flash-Preview, Mistral-Small-4, and Grok-4.2-Reasoning. A Type 0–5 failure taxonomy separates reasoning-level sycophancy from answer-level sycophancy. A sentence-level drift taxonomy then locates where capitulation starts: Visual Evidence Reading, Reasoning and Derivation, Uncertainty Expression and Reconsideration, User Belief Acknowledgment, or Answer Commitment. This design is stronger than final-answer scoring because it distinguishes perception drift, derivation drift, and last-step reversal.5f:T519,For each intended theorem T, the authors construct a complete shadow set 𝒮={S1,...,Sn}. Each shadow theorem Si is chosen so that T implies Si, giving a forward checker. The set is complete only if the conjunction S1∧...∧Sn implies T, giving a backward checker. Both directions are encoded and mechanically verified in Lean, so completeness is not an informal annotation claim but a machine-checked property. During evaluation, the generated candidate theorem \hat{T} is appended with these checkers. It receives credit only if it type-checks and passes the implication tests induced by the shadow set. A notable design choice is the annotation workflow: experts do not write everything from scratch. LLMs first draft candidate shadows, experts revise them, and Lean verifies completeness. This keeps expert labor focused on correction and validation rather than blank-page authoring. The method is especially well suited to multi-conclusion theorems, bundled conditions, existence/uniqueness statements, and other structures where partial formalization can still compile. Compared with BEq+-style reference-based equivalence checks, SA-Pass is less tied to one canonical expression. Compared with compile rate, it explicitly tests whether the generated statement is neither too weak nor too strong.60:T51b,Three results matter most. First, the benchmark: ShadowBench contains 178 Lean 4 full-autoformalization problems across eight mathematical areas and three difficulty levels, ranging from postgraduate to research level. The reference formalizations are on average about 1.6× longer than those in earlier short-form benchmarks, reflecting a stronger emphasis on multi-conclusion and structurally richer theorems. Second, metric validity: across outputs from six agentic configurations, SA-Pass achieves 98.8% binary agreement with expert judgments, versus 17.8% for compile rate and 80.6% for BEq+. The low agreement of compile rate is the key point: it cannot separate semantically wrong but compilable statements from genuinely correct ones. Third, model performance: Claude Code (Opus 4.8) with Numina-Lean-Agent gets 61.8% compile rate but only 11.2% SA-Pass on ShadowBench, a drop of more than 50 points. The paper also analyzes common failure modes, including proving only part of a bundled conclusion, turning existential claims into universal ones, omitting side conditions, and replacing equivalence with one-way implication. An earlier 126-problem version was already used in the ICML 2026 AI4Math Challenge Track 4, which gives the benchmark some external validation beyond an internal case study.61:T588,The method is a staged verification pipeline. First, an LLM rewrites the original problem using strategies such as numerical reparameterization, logical restructuring, constraint modification, and contextual reconstruction. Importantly, the rewriter is instructed not to solve the rewritten problem, which helps separate problem generation from answer generation. Second, RePro performs conservative semantic screening. This stage filters out candidates that are ambiguous, under-specified, contradictory, unrealistic, or infeasible. The paper is careful about the notion of feasibility: it is not merely formal derivability, but semantic and constraint consistency of the rewritten problem. Third, the surviving candidates are translated into executable Lean specifications, and Lean-oriented neural ATPs such as Goedel-Prover and DeepSeek-Prover search for candidate proof scripts. A proof is accepted only if it passes Lean kernel-level verification.

This design differs from prior rewriting-based evaluation in three ways. It verifies answers through formal proof rather than heuristic checking. It evaluates reliability along three axes—well-definedness, feasibility, and answer correctness—rather than treating validity as a single vague notion. And it explicitly trades recall for precision by retaining only proof-verified instances. That trade-off is deliberate and sensible for benchmark construction.62:T4a3,The experiments are conducted on GSM8K and MATH. The headline result is straightforward: among the retained rewritten instances, RePro achieves 100% well-definedness, feasibility, and answer correctness, whereas prior rewriting methods still leave invalid questions or incorrect reference answers in the benchmark. This is the central empirical claim, and it supports the paper’s argument that formal verification changes the reliability ceiling of rewritten evaluation sets.

A second important result concerns reformulation sensitivity. Using proof-verified rewrites, the authors show that several models suffer noticeable accuracy drops when mathematically equivalent problems are restated in new forms. Because the rewritten items are verified, the drop is more plausibly attributed to sensitivity to formulation and possible memorization dependence, rather than to benchmark corruption. The paper also makes clear that not every rewrite survives the pipeline: the released benchmark is a retained subset of candidates that can be formalized and proved. That gives high precision, but limits coverage and may bias the benchmark toward problems that are easier to formalize in Lean.63:T8cb,方法分两层。底层是 Active Statistical Inference（ASI），上层是作者提出的 Failure-Space Analysis（FSA）来设计抽样策略。ASI 的作用，是把“judge 对全量样本的预测”和“少量人工标签”结合起来，构造一个对 human-defined FAR 有效的估计器。直观上，它不是直接相信 judge，也不是只靠人工均匀抽样，而是用 judge 作为控制变量或辅助信号，再用带 inclusion probability 的人工抽样去校正残差。这样做的关键好处是：只要抽样概率已知，估计仍然锚定在人类标签定义的目标上，并且可以做方差控制。

真正有信息量的是 FSA。作者没有把 annotation policy 简化成“挑 judge 最不确定的样本”，而是先分析 factuality judge 的典型失配空间，再把这些失配风险转成可预测特征。全文里这套 pipeline 大致包括几类信号：
1. judge output features：例如 claim-level verdict 分布、解释文本、局部不一致、拒判或 unverifiable 模式；
2. evidence quality features：证据是否完整、是否存在时间失配、是否冲突、是否只提供弱支持；
3. task/input strata：不同 query 类型、回答长度、claim 密度、检索来源等；
4. answer-rubric alignment：回答是否需要释义、归纳、容忍轻微措辞偏差，或者是否触发 judge 过于字面对齐的问题。

这些特征不是直接拿来做最终分类，而是用来估计“judge-human residual risk”，也就是 judge 可能错到什么程度、错在哪些区域。然后作者把 residual risk 转成 ASI 的 sampling policy，让高风险区域有更高被人工标注的概率。这里的设计取舍很清楚：如果直接训练一个替代 judge 的复杂模型，容易把目标从 human-anchored inference 变成另一个黑盒预测器；而 FSA 只负责抽样，不改最终 estimand，因此更稳。

从全文表述看，这篇工作更像“统计估计 + 误差结构工程化建模”的结合，而不是单纯 active learning。active learning 通常追求提升分类器本身；这里追求的是在固定预算下更准确地估计总体 FAR，并给出有效不确定性区间。这一点和很多 LLM eval 论文不同。64:T77f,The method has two layers. The lower layer is Active Statistical Inference (ASI), and the upper layer is the paper’s Failure-Space Analysis (FSA) for annotation-policy design. ASI combines judge predictions on all examples with human labels on a sampled subset to estimate the human-defined factual accuracy rate (FAR). Intuitively, the judge acts as an auxiliary signal rather than a replacement target, and the sampled human labels correct the residual. Because the sampling probabilities are known, the estimator remains anchored to the human target and admits valid uncertainty estimates.

The more interesting contribution is FSA. Instead of reducing annotation policy to “sample low-confidence judge outputs,” the paper analyzes the structure of factuality-specific judge failures and turns that structure into predictive signals. The feature space includes at least four families: (1) judge-output features, such as claim-level verdict patterns and uncertainty cues; (2) evidence-quality features, such as incompleteness, temporal mismatch, conflict, or only indirect support; (3) task and input strata, such as query type and answer characteristics; and (4) answer-rubric alignment features, capturing cases where humans tolerate paraphrase or inference but the judge applies a more literal verification rule.

These features are used to estimate residual-risk regions, i.e., where judge-human disagreement is likely to be large. That residual-risk estimate is then converted into an ASI sampling policy, assigning higher inclusion probabilities to examples more likely to need human correction. This is an important design choice. The paper does not train a more complex replacement judge; it keeps the target fixed and improves the sampling design. That makes the method closer to statistically valid active inference than to standard active learning, whose goal is often to improve a classifier itself.65:T631,The experiments are conducted on two settings: an internal AutoFA system for virtual-assistant factuality evaluation, and the public RAGTruth benchmark with human span-level hallucination annotations. The first empirical finding is that judge-only FAR substantially underestimates human-annotated FAR, confirming that automatic factuality estimates are biased in a systematic direction.

The main result is annotation efficiency. Aggregated across budgets, FSA-guided ASI yields an average effective sample size (ESS) gain of 40.3% on AutoFA and 27.1% on RAGTruth relative to the baselines. ESS is the right metric here because the goal is not just a better point estimate, but lower-variance human-anchored estimation under a fixed labeling budget.

The comparisons include uniform sampling, confidence-based sampling, and FSA-derived policies. Confidence-based sampling improves over uniform sampling, but still trails FSA because factuality residuals are not concentrated only in low-confidence cases. The paper also presents failure-mode analyses showing that confidently wrong judge decisions are common in cases involving incomplete evidence, temporal mismatch, indirect support, and rubric misalignment.

A useful aspect of the evaluation is that the paper cares about coverage and statistical validity, not only efficiency. The claim is not “sample hard cases and hope for the best,” but “sample informative cases while preserving valid human-anchored inference.” From an engineering perspective, that is often more actionable than trying to fully eliminate judge bias.66:T506,This is a skim paper, but several parts are worth focused reading. Start with the Introduction and Background. The important shift is how the paper reframes factuality evaluation as judge-assisted but human-anchored inference. That framing is more valuable than the FAR definition itself.

Then read the method section around the ASI estimator and inclusion probabilities. You do not need every derivation, but you should understand why the estimator can use judge predictions without changing the target away from human labels.

The most important section is the FSA policy-design pipeline. Look for the failure taxonomy, the feature construction, and how residual-risk signals are mapped into sampling probabilities. That is where the paper’s practical novelty sits.

In the experiments, prioritize the plots comparing judge FAR vs human FAR, the ESS or confidence-interval comparisons across sampling policies, and the failure-mode case studies. If time is limited, those figures are enough to capture the main message. Expected reading time is about 25 to 35 minutes.

For readers working on pretraining or data quality, it is worth asking whether the same residual-risk sampling idea can be reused for data filtering audits, synthetic-data validation, or reward-model evaluation.67:T7cc,方法上，作者构造了一个四类动作空间：tool_call、ask、refuse、confirm，并把模型每一轮输出映射到其中一类；若输出没有明确决策信号，则落到 residual 的 other 类，但 GAR 不计入 other。分类规则采用固定优先级 tool_call > refuse > ask > confirm > other，tool_call 由语法判断，其余三类由文本 cue 识别。关键设计是 case-level、any-turn 的 Gold Action Recall（GAR）：对某个 benchmark category，若模型在任意一轮曾发出该场景所需的 gold action class，就算命中。它不关心轨迹最终是否通过，只问模型有没有在合适场景下做出过正确动作类型。然后把 GAR 与 benchmark 原有的 conversation accuracy（Acc）配对分析。若 grader 真正要求先做出 gold action 才能通过，则应有 Acc ≤ GAR；一旦出现 Acc > GAR，说明 grader 掩盖了动作类型错误，属于 bound violation。反过来，如果 GAR 远高于 Acc，则说明模型动作类型选对了，但后续执行、参数、状态推进出了问题。这个分解把“校准错”和“执行错”变成两个近似正交的失败模式。

作者还设计了两个推理时干预来验证机制。SRI（State-Reconciliation Intervention）针对漏掉 tool_call 的情况，通过上下文扰动去促使模型补做工具调用；CRI（Call-Reconciliation Intervention）针对不该调用却调用的情况，分成 retry 和 bypass 两种：retry 让模型重新选择动作，测试 emission 是否向 gold class 回归；bypass 则不改 emission，而是绕过不必要调用，观察轨迹分数是否恢复。这个设计的好处是，它不只是报告“模型错了”，而是在问：错误来自动作分布本身，还是来自执行链条；以及这种错误在 inference-time 是否具有可塑性。相比普通 benchmark slicing，这里更像是把 tool-use 评测从 end-to-end pass/fail 变成了 decision layer + execution layer 的分层诊断。68:T77f,The method defines a four-way action space: tool_call, ask, refuse, and confirm. Each model emission is mapped into one class using a fixed priority order: tool_call > refuse > ask > confirm > other. Tool calls are identified syntactically, while the other classes are detected through textual cues. The key metric is Gold Action Recall (GAR), computed at the case level with any-turn aggregation: if the model emits the gold action class at any turn in the case, the case counts as recalled. GAR ignores whether the full trajectory eventually passes. It only asks whether the model ever made the contextually appropriate action decision.

GAR is then paired with the benchmark’s conversation accuracy (Acc). If passing the benchmark truly requires taking the gold action, one should have Acc <= GAR. A violation, Acc > GAR, indicates grader masking: the benchmark passes trajectories that never emitted the required action class. Conversely, large slack, GAR >> Acc, indicates that the model selected the right action class but failed later in tool choice, arguments, or state progression. This decomposition turns a single end-to-end score into two approximately orthogonal failure modes.

To probe causality, the paper introduces two inference-time interventions. State-Reconciliation Intervention (SRI) targets missed tool calls by perturbing context when the gold action is tool_call but the model emitted none. Call-Reconciliation Intervention (CRI) targets unwarranted tool calls when the gold action is non-call. CRI has two variants: retry, which asks the model to re-decide and tests whether emissions move toward the gold class, and bypass, which avoids the unnecessary call without changing the emission itself. This is a strong design choice because it tests not only whether calibration is poor, but also whether it is plastic and whether fixing the decision layer actually improves trajectory outcomes.69:T5dd,The main evaluation is on BFCL v3 multi-turn, with replication on tau-squared-bench retail and airline settings. The headline result is that some models with high aggregate accuracy have very low GAR on categories that require asking or refusing. The clearest example in the paper is xLAM: 71.8% aggregate accuracy, but only 19.5% GAR on miss_param, with a 64.5-point gap relative to size-matched peers, while BFCL’s state grader still marks many such cases as PASS. That directly supports the claim that aggregate accuracy hides action miscalibration.

The authors also run a 200-case manual audit and report inter-annotator agreement of kappa = 0.92, which strengthens confidence that the diagnostic is not an artifact of noisy labeling. The same pattern appears on a second benchmark, suggesting the issue is not specific to one grader implementation.

The intervention results are especially informative. First, calibration is plastic, but heterogeneously so: the same SRI perturbation can improve Acc for one model family and hurt another. Second, CRI cleanly separates two mechanisms. Retry often shifts emissions toward the gold action class, but tends to reduce final trajectory accuracy across nearly all families. Bypass, in contrast, can preserve or improve trajectory accuracy without changing the emission. That implies that re-deciding the action is not always the right fix; in some systems, isolating or bypassing the bad call is more effective than forcing a second generation step.6a:T69a,The paper has three technical components. First, an audit of shipped judge configurations. The authors inspect 8 popular evaluation frameworks, 9 packages, and 27 default configurations. Their criterion for true commit-first is strict: the judge must produce its own parseable answer before seeing the candidate, and the final decision must be based on matching against that committed answer rather than a holistic score after joint inspection. Under this definition, none of the default configurations qualify; several implement variants already known to be ineffective.

Second, a controlled optimization setup based on plain best-of-N selection. This is important because the attack is not exotic. The system simply samples multiple candidates and keeps the one preferred by the judge, without access to ground truth during selection. On a real coding task, this is enough to game a shipped judge configuration: measured score rises while true correctness does not. Replacing the shipped judge with commit-first removes the effect on that task.

Third, the paper isolates the residual failure mode. On tasks the judge cannot solve reliably, commit-first causes optimization to converge toward the judge’s own wrong committed answer. The judged system no longer learns to flatter the evaluator; it learns to reproduce the evaluator’s mistake. The authors then propose a cheap pre-deployment probe: ask the judge to solve the task directly and score those answers against hidden checks. This predicts when commit-first will help and when it will backfire. A useful conceptual point follows: judge competence is a property of the judge-task pair, not a monotonic function of model size.6b:T4dc,The most important numbers come in three groups. First, from prior measured baselines used to motivate the audit: when the candidate is visible during reasoning, false positive rate on wrong answers can remain as high as 0.719; true commit-first can reduce it to 0.012. Second, from the software audit: across 8 frameworks and 27 default judge configurations, none implement full commit-first, and 9 implement variants the literature already found ineffective. Third, from the optimization experiments: plain best-of-N selection reliably games a shipped judge on a real coding task across two seeds; commit-first removes that effect when the judge can solve the task, but makes outcomes worse when the judge cannot. In one seed, the final population correctness nearly matches the correctness of the judge’s committed answer, showing that optimization is tightly bounded by judge competence.

A notable empirical observation is that gaming is more reproducible than the repair. The failure mode replicates tightly across seeds, while the benefit of the defense is task-dependent and less stable. Another useful result is that larger models do not automatically make commit-first safe; the decisive variable is competence on the specific task.6c:T410,For a skim, focus on four parts. Start with the introduction and contribution list, which already state the central claim clearly: commit-first moves the anchor of optimization rather than removing it. Then read the audit section to see how the paper distinguishes genuine commit-first from look-alike implementations. After that, go to the best-of-N experiments, because they show that ordinary selection pressure is enough to exploit a judge. Finally, read the direct-solve probe section, which is the most actionable part if you build evaluator-dependent training loops.

If time is limited, prioritize the definition of the audit criteria, the coding-task optimization experiment, and the hidden-check / reachability methodology. Around 20–30 minutes should be enough to extract the main lessons. The deeper questions worth following up are whether judge ensembles can reduce inherited-error collapse, and whether direct-solve competence can be turned into an automatic gate before using a judge inside RL or synthetic-data pipelines.6d:Ta85,方法上，这篇工作核心不是提出新模型，而是搭了一套面向 dLVLM 的系统评测与机制分析框架。评测对象包括 6 个 diffusion LVLM：LLaDA-V、LaViDa-LLaDA、LaViDa-Dream、MMaDA-MixCoT、Dream-VL、Dimple，并与 7 个有竞争力的 AR LVLM 做对比。四类评测分别对应不同失效模式。

在 object hallucination 上，作者用 POPE，在 Random、Popular、Adversarial 三种采样设置下报告 Accuracy、Precision、Recall、F1 和 Yes%。这里 Yes% 很关键，因为它直接暴露回答倾向。结果显示 AR 模型常见的 affirmative bias 在 dLVLM 上被明显改写，很多 diffusion 模型更偏向否定回答，形成一种“yes-bias reversal”。这不是简单的阈值问题，因为它在多个模型家族上重复出现。

在 open-ended hallucination 上，作者用 CHAIR 评估自由 caption，并把 hallucination rate 与语言质量拆开分析。结论不是“dLVLM 更会幻觉”，而是“它们的 hallucination rate 可以接近 AR，但语言质量更差”，说明 diffusion 生成中的迭代去噪和并行提交机制，可能在 grounding 与表面语言组织之间引入了新的张力。

在 demographic bias 上，作者用 FairFace 做 gender / race 识别，并在两种 padding 条件下测试。这里的发现比较尖锐：对 underrepresented racial groups，部分 dLVLM 准确率接近塌缩到零；同时不同 diffusion 家族出现相反方向的 gender bias，而不是统一偏向某一类。这说明偏置不只是数据分布问题，也和具体 backbone、视觉接入方式、后训练策略有关。

在 selection bias 上，作者构造了长度受控的视觉多选题，专门测选项长度是否成为混杂线索。结果显示 dLVLM 的长度偏置显著强于 AR，而且作者进一步把这种偏置追到 first denoising step：模型在最早一轮去噪时就对较长选项表现出系统性偏好，后续步骤更多是在强化而不是纠正这个早期决定。

机制分析部分是全文最有信息量的地方。作者利用 diffusion 推断天然可见的两个过程信号：per-token confidence trajectory，以及 token 的 commit step。commit step 指 token 第一次被赋予最终非 mask 值的时刻。作者发现 hallucinated content 往往伴随特定的置信度轨迹和提交模式，这意味着 dLVLM 比 AR 多了一类可观测的内部诊断信号。AR 模型通常只能看最终 token probability，而 diffusion 模型可以看“这个 token 在第几步被定下来、之后是否稳定、置信度如何演化”，这为后续做 hallucination detection、early stopping、selective regeneration 提供了接口。6e:T9ac,This is an evaluation and analysis paper rather than a new model paper, but the setup is carefully designed for diffusion LVLMs. The authors benchmark six diffusion models—LLaDA-V, LaViDa-LLaDA, LaViDa-Dream, MMaDA-MixCoT, Dream-VL, and Dimple—against seven competitive autoregressive LVLM baselines.

For object hallucination, they use POPE under Random, Popular, and Adversarial settings, reporting Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1, and Yes%. Yes% is central because it exposes response tendency directly. A consistent pattern is that many diffusion models reverse the familiar AR yes-bias in binary visual questions, often becoming overly negative instead of overly affirmative.

For open-ended hallucination, they use CHAIR on free-form captioning and explicitly separate hallucination rate from linguistic quality. The key result is not that diffusion models hallucinate more across the board, but that they can achieve competitive hallucination rates while producing weaker language. This suggests that iterative denoising and parallel token commitment alter the trade-off between grounding and surface fluency.

For demographic bias, they evaluate gender and race recognition on FairFace under two padding conditions. The striking observation is near-collapse on underrepresented racial groups for some diffusion models, together with opposite-polarity gender bias across model families. That points to an interaction between the diffusion paradigm and implementation choices such as the base LM, vision integration, and post-training recipe.

For selection bias, they build length-controlled visual MCQA instances to test whether option length becomes a confounding cue. Diffusion models show much stronger length bias than AR baselines. More interestingly, the bias appears already at the first denoising step, which means the model forms a skewed preference very early and later iterations mostly reinforce it.

The mechanistic part is the most informative section. Diffusion inference exposes process signals that AR models do not naturally provide: per-token confidence trajectories and token commit steps. A commit step is the denoising step at which a token first receives its final non-mask value. The paper shows that hallucinated content correlates with characteristic confidence and commitment patterns. That creates a practical interface for future work on hallucination detection, selective regeneration, and inference-time calibration in diffusion LMs.6f:T6b8,The experimental contribution is more about stable patterns than about one headline number. The study covers 6 diffusion LVLMs, 7 AR baselines, and four evaluation suites: POPE, CHAIR, FairFace, and length-controlled MCQA.

The first major result is the reversal of yes-bias on POPE. AR LVLMs often over-answer “yes” under uncertainty, while many diffusion models lean toward “no.” This changes the precision-recall balance: some diffusion models maintain reasonable precision but lose recall because they become too conservative.

The second result is on CHAIR. Diffusion models can be competitive with strong AR baselines in hallucination rate, yet their linguistic quality is noticeably worse. The paper argues that hallucination and language quality are separable failure dimensions, which is an important evaluation lesson.

The third result comes from FairFace. Some diffusion models show near-zero accuracy on underrepresented racial groups, and gender bias is not even consistent in direction across model families. This indicates that reliability behavior is highly implementation-dependent rather than a single generic property of diffusion.

The fourth result is the strong length bias in visual MCQA. Diffusion models are much more sensitive to answer-option length than AR baselines, and the analysis traces this effect to the first denoising step. That early-step commitment is one of the clearest mechanistic findings in the paper.

The paper also includes analyses under different padding conditions and studies the correlation between confidence trajectories and hallucinated tokens. The exact numbers matter less than the fact that these patterns recur across multiple model families and tasks.70:T67a,The method is PTA-IRT, short for Privileged Trajectory-Aware Item Response Theory. It extends standard IRT in two ways: trajectory-aware item calibration and LUPI-based ability estimation.

First, the framework collects historical execution trajectories from prior agents on the benchmark. Instead of feeding raw logs directly, it converts them into structured semantic summaries that capture process-level signals such as context exploration, edit attempts, tool usage, and verification paths. These summaries are then used to learn trajectory-aware item characteristics under a four-parameter logistic (4PL) IRT model. Compared with simpler 2PL or 3PL variants, 4PL offers more flexibility for asymmetric success curves that are common in agent tasks.

Second, for subset selection, PTA-IRT uses trajectory-aware Fisher information to choose a difficulty-stratified calibration subset. The goal is not merely to pick tasks that separate agents by final outcome, but to pick tasks whose process patterns are informative for ability estimation.

Third, at test time, a new agent only needs to run on the selected calibration subset. The full historical trajectory information is not required online. Through Learning Using Privileged Information (LUPI), the system transfers trajectory-side knowledge learned offline into an estimator that can infer full-benchmark performance from limited calibration observations.

A practical strength of the setup is the protocol itself: trajectories are privileged only during offline training, while online evaluation remains cheap. That makes the method consistent with the original goal of reducing benchmarking cost.71:T4e1,The experiments are conducted on four SWE benchmarks and compare PTA-IRT against prior IRT baselines. The main result is consistent across datasets: under low calibration budgets, PTA-IRT improves both score recovery and ranking recovery over outcome-only methods. In other words, the gains are strongest exactly where efficient evaluation matters most.

The ablations are important. Removing trajectory information and keeping only pass/fail outcomes or static task semantics weakens performance, which shows that the improvement comes from process signals rather than just a more complex estimator. Corrupting or degrading the trajectory summaries also hurts recovery, suggesting that the model is using meaningful solving-path information rather than simply benefiting from longer text inputs. The paper further compares issue text, submitted patches, and structured trajectory summaries, and finds that the structured summaries carry additional measurement value.

From a research perspective, the key takeaway is not a single absolute number but the regime where the method helps: low-budget evaluation. If one can afford full-benchmark runs, subset estimation is unnecessary. PTA-IRT is useful precisely when evaluation cost is the bottleneck.72:T418,For a skim read, start with the task formulation and protocol figure to make sure the paper is about budgeted subset-to-full evaluation, not about improving the agent itself. Then read the method overview and keep the three stages in mind: trajectory summarization, trajectory-aware 4PL calibration, and LUPI-based ability estimation. Finally, inspect the low-budget result plots and the ablations to see whether the gains are robust.

If you only have 20 to 30 minutes, prioritize the method diagram, the main tables or plots showing score/rank recovery at different budgets, and the ablation that removes trajectory summaries. If you are not familiar with IRT, it is enough to understand how difficulty, discrimination, and latent ability are refined by trajectory information; the full derivation is not necessary for a first pass.

This paper is most relevant for people working on agent evaluation or benchmark design. For pretraining researchers, the useful lesson is methodological: process signals can be more informative than final labels.73:T816,The core method is XTE, Cross-Modal Temporal Edits. Starting from an original video-text pair (V, y), the authors define a family of temporal edit operators A_k and matching caption rewrite functions g_k. On the video side, edits include clip reversal, event reordering, and temporal masking. On the text side, the caption is synchronously rewritten with temporal markers such as before, after, and reversed. The result is a paired temporal counterfactual: the edited video and edited text remain semantically aligned, while differing from the original pair only in chronology. That is the key design choice. Because the original and edited videos share nearly the same frames, static spatial cues are held constant, and the model is forced to rely on temporal structure rather than appearance shortcuts.

On the model side, ViTAL-X does not retrain a large video model from scratch. It starts from frozen image-text backbones such as OpenCLIP or SigLIP-2, then adds a shallow spatiotemporal transformer to model cross-frame dependencies, together with targeted LoRA fine-tuning. The trade-off is clear: preserve the strong static semantic priors learned from large-scale image-text pretraining, inject temporal modeling only where needed, avoid catastrophic forgetting, and keep training efficient.

The training objective is contrastive learning over XTE-generated hard negatives. The novelty is not the loss form itself, but the negative distribution. Standard video-text contrastive learning uses unrelated videos as negatives, which differ in actors, objects, and scenes, allowing the model to solve the task through static shortcuts. XTE replaces those with temporal counterfactuals of the same video, so static appearance is no longer sufficient.

The paper also introduces XTE-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark aimed specifically at temporal order, direction, and causality. That evaluation asset is important because standard benchmarks often let models score well through spatial bias, making it hard to verify whether temporal understanding has actually improved.74:T5d0,From the provided full-text content, the main empirical claims are threefold.

First, XTE-Bench reveals that current large video-language models remain weak on basic temporal reasoning, even when they are large. This supports the paper’s main argument that temporal blindness is not automatically fixed by parameter scaling.

Second, ViTAL-X is positioned as highly efficient. The paper claims that a roughly 0.4B-parameter model trained on only 1M clips can outperform some 7B-parameter models and baselines trained on about 600 times more data. The important point is not only the headline comparison, but the implication: when the failure mode comes from the wrong objective and the wrong negative distribution, scaling alone has poor marginal returns.

Third, the method is reported to generalize beyond the custom diagnostic benchmark to multiple independent video-understanding benchmarks. If the main tables support that claim, it suggests that XTE is not merely overfitting to a narrow family of temporal edits, but is improving temporal representation more broadly.

The excerpt does not include full tables or exact benchmark scores, so the most important things to verify in a full read are the ablations: which temporal edit operators matter most, how much gain comes from the shallow temporal module versus LoRA, and whether static semantic performance is preserved. Those details determine whether the method is a robust training recipe or just a benchmark-specific trick.75:T5ad,Read it with two questions in mind: is the failure truly structural, and does the method really isolate time as the only changing variable? Start with the introduction’s definition of temporal blindness and the explanation of why pooling-based video adaptation erases order information. Then go straight to the XTE construction in the methods. The key issue is not how many edit types are listed, but whether the video edits and caption rewrites are tightly synchronized and whether they alter only temporal structure.

After that, inspect the ViTAL-X architecture. Focus on where the shallow spatiotemporal transformer is inserted, which modules receive LoRA, and why the backbone is frozen instead of fully fine-tuned. In the experiments, prioritize the design of XTE-Bench and the main result tables, then the transfer benchmarks and ablations. If time is limited, 20 to 30 minutes is enough to capture the main argument. A deeper read is needed if the goal is to assess whether this can inform unified multimodal pretraining.

Three questions are worth probing further. First, are the rewritten captions natural enough, or do they introduce templated lexical cues that the model can exploit?
